name: Rome
blurb: From Julius Caesar to the fall of the West in 476
dateConvention: Dates are Julian, as Roman sources give them. BC years count down with no year zero, and many third-century reigns are known only to the month or year.
epilogue: In the West, the emperors were gone. In the East they ruled on from Constantinople for nearly a thousand years more, until the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

reigns.tagline: He crossed a river and the Republic never recovered
reigns.cameToPower: Crossed the Rubicon, won a civil war
reigns.reignEnded: Stabbed on the Ides of March
reigns.previously: Rome is a republic run by rival generals, mobs and a nervous Senate.
paragraphs: By 49 BC Caesar had spent nine years conquering Gaul and getting very rich. His enemies in the Senate ordered him to give up his army and come home to face the courts. He came home, all right. In January he led his troops over the Rubicon, the little river that marked the edge of Italy, and that act alone meant civil war.

His old partner Pompey fled east. Caesar chased him and beat him at Pharsalus in 48 BC. Pompey ran to Egypt, where courtiers of the boy king cut off his head. Caesar arrived anyway, sided with the young queen Cleopatra, and had a son with her. Then he mopped up the last Pompeians in Africa and Spain.

Back in Rome he fixed the calendar, which still shapes ours, and handed out land to his veterans. In early 44 BC he became dictator for life. To many senators that sounded like a king. On 15 March, at a Senate meeting, a gang of them led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed him 23 times.

claims.text: As he died, Caesar said "Et tu, Brute?" to his friend Brutus.
claims.note: That Latin line is Shakespeare's. Suetonius says Caesar died silent, though some claimed he said "You too, child?" in Greek.

claims.text: Crossing the Rubicon, he said "The die is cast."
claims.note: Suetonius gives the line in Latin; Plutarch says he quoted it in Greek from the poet Menander. Both wrote over 150 years later.

claims.text: A soothsayer warned him to beware the Ides of March.
claims.note: Suetonius names the seer Spurinna and says the warning came weeks earlier. It's a good story told after the fact.

reigns.hook: Caesar lies dead at the foot of Pompey's statue. The killers expect cheering crowds. Instead they get Mark Antony, Caesar's fellow consul, and a funeral that will set Rome on fire.

reigns.title: Mark Antony
reigns.tagline: Caesar's right-hand man grabs the wheel
reigns.previously: Caesar is stabbed to death in the Senate on the Ides of March, 44 BC.
paragraphs: On the Ides of March Antony was consul, the one man with real authority still standing. The killers spared him, and at first he played it calm, agreeing an amnesty with the Senate. Then came Caesar's funeral. Antony read out the will and stirred up the crowd, and Rome went wild. The mob burned the body in the Forum and went hunting for the assassins. Within weeks Brutus and Cassius had slipped out of the city.

Antony took charge of Caesar's papers and money, and looked set to inherit his power. Then an 18-year-old arrived from across the Adriatic calling himself Caesar. Octavian was Caesar's great-nephew and adopted son, and he wanted the money Caesar had left the people. Antony brushed him off. Octavian raised a private army from Caesar's veterans, and Cicero, in a run of furious speeches, turned the Senate against Antony.

In April 43 BC the Senate's armies, with Octavian's men alongside, beat Antony at Mutina in northern Italy. Both consuls died in the fighting, and Antony retreated over the Alps, where Lepidus and the governors of Gaul joined him. Octavian marched on Rome and made himself consul at 19. Then he switched sides. That autumn the three men met on a river island near Bononia (Bologna) and agreed to run the Roman world together.

claims.text: Antony's funeral speech began "Friends, Romans, countrymen".
claims.note: Those words are Shakespeare's. Suetonius says Antony added only a few words of his own; Appian and Plutarch give him a big emotional scene.

claims.text: Cicero's speeches against Antony are called the Philippics, after Demosthenes' attacks on Philip of Macedon.
claims.note: Fourteen of them survive. Cicero chose the name himself, half as a joke.

claims.text: On the retreat over the Alps Antony drank foul water and ate wild roots like his men.
claims.note: Plutarch tells it, about 150 years later. He liked to show Antony at his best when things were at their worst.

reigns.hook: Three men, one deal. Antony, Octavian and Lepidus are about to become a legal dictatorship, and their first job is to draw up a list of names. Cicero's is on it.

reigns.title: Antony & Octavian
reigns.tagline: Two heirs of Caesar, one world, and no room to share it
reigns.cameToPower: Lex Titia: five years of legal power
reigns.previously: Antony, Octavian and Lepidus agree to share power near Bononia.
paragraphs: The Lex Titia of 27 November 43 BC made the three men triumvirs, with power to make laws and pick officials for five years. Their first act was a kill list. Hundreds of senators and rich men were proscribed, and their property paid the troops. Antony insisted on Cicero. On 7 December soldiers caught the old orator near his villa at Formiae and cut off his head and hands, which were put on show in the Forum.

In October 42 BC Antony and Octavian crushed Brutus and Cassius in two battles at Philippi in Greece, and both killers took their own lives. The partners split the empire. Antony took the rich East and in 41 BC summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus. She sailed up the river in a gilded barge. Octavian got Italy and the thankless job of settling veterans. Lepidus got Africa, and in 36 BC lost everything after a failed grab for Sicily.

Antony's Parthian war went badly, and at the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BC he handed out eastern lands to Cleopatra and her children. Octavian made sure Rome heard about it. In 32 BC he declared war on Cleopatra alone. At Actium, on 2 September 31 BC, Agrippa won the sea battle and the lovers fled to Egypt. When Octavian took Alexandria on 1 August 30 BC, Antony fell on his sword. Cleopatra died days later.

claims.text: Cleopatra killed herself with the bite of an asp smuggled in a basket of figs.
claims.note: Plutarch tells it but admits nobody knew the truth. Poison is just as likely; no snake was found.

claims.text: Antony's will, seized by Octavian, asked for him to be buried in Alexandria beside Cleopatra.
claims.note: Plutarch and Cassius Dio say Octavian took it from the Vestal Virgins and read it out. Some historians suspect he doctored it.

claims.text: Antony's wife Fulvia stabbed the dead Cicero's tongue with her hairpin.
claims.note: Only Cassius Dio tells this, about 250 years later. That Cicero's head and hands were shown in the Forum is well attested.

reigns.hook: Antony is dead and Lepidus is a has-been. Octavian, aged 32, is alone with the treasure of Egypt and every legion in the empire. One loose end is left: Cleopatra's teenage son by Julius Caesar.

reigns.title: Octavian, alone
reigns.tagline: He won everything, then offered to give it all back
reigns.previously: Antony falls on his sword as Octavian takes Alexandria.
paragraphs: Octavian had won, but he moved carefully. Cleopatra was dead, and so was Caesarion, her 17-year-old son by Julius Caesar, killed on Octavian's orders. Egypt became a Roman province run by Octavian's own man, and senators needed his permission even to visit it. Its treasure paid off his soldiers and bought them land.

In August 29 BC he rode through Rome in a triple triumph, three days of parades for Illyricum, Actium and Egypt. The doors of the temple of Janus were shut, the sign that Rome was at peace, for only the third time in its history. He was consul every year and the armies answered to him alone. Everyone knew who was in charge. The question was what to call it.

Caesar had been murdered for looking like a king, and Octavian had learned the lesson. In January 27 BC he told the Senate he was handing the state back to the Senate and People of Rome. The senators begged him to stay on. He kindly agreed to keep a huge province, with most of the legions in it. On 16 January they voted him a new name: Augustus.

claims.text: A courtier talked him into killing Caesarion with a pun: "Too many Caesars is no good."
claims.note: Plutarch credits the line to the philosopher Arius. Caesarion's death is certain; the clever remark is hard to check.

claims.text: Visiting Alexander the Great's tomb, he knocked a bit off the mummy's nose.
claims.note: Only Cassius Dio tells it, over 200 years later. Suetonius has him lay a crown and flowers on the body, and says nothing of a nose.

claims.text: He shut the doors of the temple of Janus, closed only twice before in Rome's history.
claims.note: Augustus says so in his own Res Gestae, and Livy agrees about the two earlier closings.

reigns.hook: Octavian has given everything back, and got it all returned with a new name. Augustus, "the revered one", now has to make a one-man state look like a republic for the next 40 years.

reigns.tagline: He ended the Republic and said he was saving it
reigns.cameToPower: Won at Actium; Senate named him
reigns.reignEnded: Died in his bed at Nola
reigns.previously: Octavian hands power back to the Senate, and is renamed Augustus.
paragraphs: In January 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian a new name: Augustus, "the revered one". He never called himself king or emperor. He was just the first citizen, who happened to command most of the army and control the treasury. Rome was tired of civil war, and almost nobody complained.

He ruled for over 40 years. He rebuilt temples, set up a fire brigade and a standing army, and pushed the frontiers to the Danube. Things went badly wrong in AD 9, when three legions under Varus were wiped out in the German forests. Augustus never tried to conquer Germany again.

His real headache was the succession. His nephew Marcellus died young, then his friend Agrippa, then his grandsons Gaius and Lucius. In the end he adopted his stepson Tiberius, the son of his wife Livia. He died in August AD 14, aged 75, and the Senate declared him a god.

claims.text: Livia poisoned him with figs smeared on the tree.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says only that some people claimed it. Tacitus hints at rumours too. There's no real evidence.

claims.text: He boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.
claims.note: Suetonius reports the boast, and the building programme behind it is real.

claims.text: After the Varus disaster he beat his head on a door, crying "Varus, give me back my legions!"
claims.note: Suetonius tells it a century later. The grief is believable; the exact scene may be dressed up.

reigns.hook: The god is dead. His heir is a gloomy, brilliant general of 55 who insists he doesn't want the job. The Senate can't tell if he means it, and that makes them very nervous.

reigns.tagline: The reluctant emperor who ruled Rome from a cliff top
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Stepson and adopted son of Augustus
reigns.previously: Augustus dies after 40 years in charge, his stepson his heir.
paragraphs: Tiberius was a fine general and a dour, suspicious man. He made a show of refusing power, which only annoyed the Senate. His popular nephew and adopted son Germanicus died in Syria in AD 19, and many Romans were sure Tiberius had wanted him gone. Then his own son Drusus died in AD 23.

More and more, Tiberius leaned on Sejanus, the commander of the Praetorian Guard. In AD 26 the emperor left Rome for good, and soon settled on the island of Capri. Sejanus ran things back home and plotted to climb higher. In AD 31 Tiberius struck first: a letter read out in the Senate brought Sejanus down, and he was executed that day.
The last years were a grim run of treason trials. Tiberius died at Misenum in March AD 37. His heir was Gaius, the young son of Germanicus, and the crowds in Rome cheered the news.

claims.text: Tiberius filled his Capri villa with sex parties and cruel games.
claims.note: Suetonius tells lurid stories, written about 80 years later by men who hated Tiberius. Historians treat them as gossip.

claims.text: As Tiberius lay dying, the guard commander Macro smothered him with a pillow.
claims.note: Tacitus gives this version; Suetonius offers poison and starvation too. Nobody agrees.

claims.text: Sejanus and Drusus's wife Livilla poisoned Drusus.
claims.note: It came out only after Sejanus fell, in a letter from his ex-wife Apicata before her suicide. Tacitus believed it.

reigns.hook: Rome throws a party for its new emperor. Gaius is 24, the son of a hero, and he's promising a fresh start. Within a year, people start to wonder about him.

reigns.tagline: Rome's darling turned Rome's nightmare in four years
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by the Senate and the Guard
reigns.previously: Old Tiberius dies at Misenum. Rome cheers his young heir.
paragraphs: His real name was Gaius. "Caligula" means "little boot", a nickname from his childhood in army camps, where he wore a tiny soldier's outfit. He started well: amnesties, games, tax cuts. Then, a few months in, he fell badly ill. After he recovered, the mood changed.

He had his cousin and co-heir Tiberius Gemellus killed. He blew through the treasury, built a bridge of boats across the bay at Baiae so he could ride over the sea, and demanded worship as a god. He marched an army to the Channel to invade Britain and then went home. He humiliated senators and guard officers for fun.

That was a mistake. On 24 January AD 41, during games on the Palatine, a guard officer named Cassius Chaerea and others cornered him in a passage and cut him down. His wife and baby daughter were killed too. The Senate talked about bringing back the Republic. The Guard had other ideas.

claims.text: Caligula planned to make his favourite horse, Incitatus, a consul.
claims.note: Suetonius says he was said to have planned it; Dio says he promised to. It reads as a joke at the Senate's expense, if it happened at all.

claims.text: At the Channel he ordered his troops to gather seashells as plunder from the sea.
claims.note: Suetonius tells it. Some historians think the word for shells may mean army huts or boats, or that the story was twisted.

claims.text: He slept with his sisters.
claims.note: Suetonius repeats it as fact, but it fits a stock smear for tyrants. Philo and Seneca, who lived through the reign, don't say so.

reigns.hook: Soldiers ransack the palace. Behind a curtain they find a pair of feet. They belong to Caligula's uncle Claudius, a stammering scholar everyone has written off. The Guard has its next emperor.

reigns.tagline: The family joke who conquered Britain
reigns.cameToPower: Found behind a curtain by guards
reigns.reignEnded: Died after a dish of mushrooms
reigns.previously: Caligula is cut down by his own guards in a palace passage.
paragraphs: Claudius limped, stammered and twitched, and his own mother called him a monster. The family hid him away, so he spent decades writing history books. That kept him alive. When the Guard made him emperor, he paid each soldier handsomely, which set a nasty habit for the future.

He turned out to be a hard-working ruler. In AD 43 his armies invaded Britain, and Claudius came over for about 16 days, bringing elephants, to collect the glory. At home he built a new harbour at Ostia and two great aqueducts, and leaned heavily on clever freedmen to run the government.

His marriages were a disaster. In AD 48 his young wife Messalina went through a wedding with her lover while Claudius was away, and was executed. Next he married his niece Agrippina, who pushed him to adopt her son Nero ahead of his own son Britannicus. In October AD 54 Claudius died suddenly.

claims.text: Agrippina killed him with a plate of poisoned mushrooms.
claims.note: Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio all say so, and the timing suits her. But they disagree on the details, and an illness can't be ruled out.

claims.text: Messalina beat a prostitute in an all-night contest to see who could take more lovers.
claims.note: Pliny the Elder tells it, and later Juvenal mocks her. It's the kind of tale told about a disgraced empress.

reigns.hook: Agrippina keeps the death quiet until everything is ready. Then the palace doors open and her son steps out to meet the Guard. Nero is 16, and his mother intends to run the show.

reigns.tagline: The singing emperor Rome blamed for the fire
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Stepson and adopted son of Claudius
reigns.cameToPower: His mother fixed it with the Guard
reigns.reignEnded: Suicide as his own Senate turned
reigns.previously: Claudius dies suddenly, and Agrippina's son is ready to take over.
paragraphs: With his tutor Seneca and the guard commander Burrus steering, Nero's early years went fairly well. The family was another matter. His stepbrother Britannicus dropped dead at dinner in AD 55. In AD 59 Nero had his mother Agrippina killed, after a boat rigged to collapse failed to drown her.

In July AD 64 a fire raged through Rome for days and gutted much of the city. Nero opened his gardens to the homeless, then blamed the Christians and had many killed horribly. On the ruins he built the Golden House, a vast palace with its own lake. Romans noticed.

A plot to kill him failed in AD 65, and Seneca was ordered to take his own life. Nero toured Greece singing and racing chariots. In AD 68 the governors in Gaul and Spain rebelled, the Guard deserted him and the Senate declared him a public enemy. On 9 June, hiding in a villa, he stabbed himself in the throat.

claims.text: Nero fiddled while Rome burned.
claims.note: There were no fiddles in Rome. Tacitus says Nero was at Antium and only rumoured to have sung about the fall of Troy.

claims.text: Nero started the Great Fire himself to clear space for his palace.
claims.note: Suetonius and Dio say so. Tacitus says nobody could tell whether it was arson or accident.

claims.text: His last words were "What an artist dies in me!"
claims.note: Suetonius reports it. It suits Nero so neatly that some suspect polish, but no one has a better source.

reigns.hook: Augustus's family line is finished. In Spain, a tough old governor of 70 named Galba is marching on Rome. He's about to discover that an emperor can be made somewhere other than Rome.

reigns.tagline: The old man who wouldn't pay the soldiers
reigns.cameToPower: Revolt in Spain; the Senate backed him
reigns.previously: Nero is dead by his own hand. Augustus's family line is finished.
paragraphs: Galba was old money: a stiff, bald, gouty aristocrat of 70 who had served emperors since Augustus. In 68 he was governing Spain when a revolt broke out in Gaul against Nero. Galba's troops hailed him, the Senate switched sides, and Nero ran out of friends. Suddenly an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome, by an army. That secret was out, and it never went back in the box.

He was famously tight with money. His agents had promised the Praetorian Guard a huge bonus. Galba refused to pay, saying he picked his soldiers and didn't buy them. On 1 January 69 the Rhine legions refused to swear loyalty and hailed their own man, Vitellius. Galba then adopted a dull young noble called Piso as his heir, snubbing his ally Otho. Five days later Otho bought the Guard, and Galba and Piso were butchered in the Forum.

claims.text: Tacitus judged that everyone would have thought Galba fit to rule, if only he had never ruled.
claims.note: It's Tacitus's own verdict in the Histories (capax imperii nisi imperasset), one of the most quoted lines in Latin.

claims.text: His last words were 'Strike, if it is for the good of Rome.'
claims.note: Tacitus gives this and a much less noble version side by side and admits nobody really knew.

claims.text: A soldier carried his severed head by sticking a thumb in its mouth, since there was no hair to grab.
claims.note: A grisly detail from Suetonius. Plutarch and Tacitus agree the head was paraded, but not on the thumb.

reigns.hook: Galba's head is on a pole and Otho has the throne he paid for. But up on the Rhine the legions have already picked another emperor, and they're marching south.

reigns.tagline: The playboy who died better than he lived
reigns.previously: Old Galba refused to pay the Guard. They cut him down in the Forum.
paragraphs: Otho had been Nero's party friend, a dandy with a wig and a taste for perfume. Then his beautiful wife Poppaea caught Nero's eye. Otho was packed off to govern faraway Lusitania (roughly modern Portugal) for ten years, and Poppaea became empress. When Galba rose against Nero, Otho backed him early and hoped to be named heir. He wasn't, so he bribed the Guard and took the throne himself.

He had no time to enjoy it. Vitellius's Rhine army was already crossing the Alps. On 14 April 69 Otho's troops lost a hard battle near Bedriacum, outside Cremona. Otho was waiting nearby at Brixellum with fresh legions on the way. He could have fought on. Instead he made a calm speech, burned his letters, slept, and at dawn stabbed himself. He had ruled for three months. Even his critics admitted he died well.

claims.text: Otho killed himself to save Rome from more civil war.
claims.note: Tacitus, Suetonius and Plutarch all say so and give him a fine farewell speech. Some historians think he simply saw the war was lost.

claims.text: His wife Poppaea left him for Nero, and Nero sent Otho to Lusitania to get him out of the way.
claims.note: All the main sources agree on the outline, though Tacitus gives two different versions of how the affair began.

claims.text: Grief-stricken soldiers killed themselves beside his funeral pyre.
claims.note: Reported by Tacitus and Suetonius. Plausible, but the scale can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Otho is dead and the Senate quickly salutes Vitellius. But the armies of the East have watched three emperors made by soldiers, and they have a candidate of their own.

reigns.tagline: The glutton emperor who lasted eight months
reigns.previously: Otho lost at Bedriacum and stabbed himself to stop the bloodshed.
paragraphs: Vitellius came from a well-connected family; his father had been consul three times. Galba sent him to command the legions in Lower Germany, which turned out to be a mistake. On 2 January 69 the troops hailed him emperor. His generals did the fighting and beat Otho while Vitellius followed at a leisurely pace, feasting all the way. In Rome he swapped the Praetorian Guard for his own German legionaries.

In July the eastern legions declared for Vespasian. The Danube armies joined in, poured into Italy and crushed Vitellius's men at a second battle near Bedriacum in October, then sacked Cremona. Vitellius tried to abdicate in December, but his own soldiers wouldn't let him. In the street fighting the great Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol burned. On 20 December the Flavian troops stormed Rome, dragged Vitellius from hiding, killed him and threw his body in the Tiber.

claims.text: He served a dish called the 'Shield of Minerva' made of pike livers, pheasant and peacock brains, flamingo tongues and lamprey milt.
claims.note: Suetonius describes it in loving detail. His account comes from the Flavian era, when blackening Vitellius was official policy.

claims.text: Visiting the battlefield, he said a dead enemy smells sweet, and a dead fellow citizen sweeter still.
claims.note: Only Suetonius has the line, and it sounds like a story made up to fit the villain.

claims.text: Vitellius's soldiers set fire to the Temple of Jupiter.
claims.note: Tacitus says it was unclear whether the attackers or the defenders started the blaze.

reigns.hook: Vitellius is in the Tiber. Rome has had four emperors in a year. The fourth is still in Egypt: a blunt old soldier, son of a tax collector, who means to make it stick.

reigns.tagline: The tough old soldier who taxed the toilets
reigns.previously: Vitellius was lynched in Rome. The Year of the Four Emperors is over.
paragraphs: Vespasian was a self-made man from Sabine country, the son of a tax man and the first of his family in the Senate. He led a legion in the invasion of Britain under Claudius and captured the Isle of Wight. Under Nero he fell out of favour for nodding off during one of the emperor's singing recitals. Still, he was sent to crush the Jewish revolt. On 1 July 69 the legions in Egypt swore loyalty to him, and the whole East followed.

He sat in Egypt, holding Rome's grain supply, while his allies took Italy. He found the treasury empty and taxed everything, even the urine collected from public toilets, which laundries used. He began the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Colosseum, on the site of Nero's private lake. He ran the empire with dry humour and no pretensions for ten years, then fell ill. He was the first emperor whose own son succeeded him.

claims.text: When his son Titus objected to the urine tax, Vespasian held a coin under his nose and asked if it smelled.
claims.note: Suetonius tells the story. The tax was real; the Latin tag 'pecunia non olet' (money doesn't stink) is a later summary.

claims.text: His deathbed joke was 'Oh dear, I think I'm becoming a god.'
claims.note: Suetonius reports it. Dead emperors were often declared gods, and it fits his famous dry wit, but nobody else confirms it.

claims.text: In Alexandria he healed a blind man with his spit.
claims.note: Tacitus and Suetonius both report it, which shows the story was spread at the time. It was handy propaganda for a new dynasty.

reigns.hook: Vespasian dies joking. For the first time, an emperor's own son takes over without a fight. Titus is charming and loved, and disaster is about to strike.

reigns.tagline: The darling of Rome, gone in two years
reigns.previously: Vespasian died joking that he was turning into a god.
paragraphs: Titus grew up at court as a friend of Claudius's son Britannicus. When Vespasian left Judaea to claim the throne, Titus took over the war. In 70 he captured Jerusalem and the Temple was destroyed; the Arch of Titus in Rome still shows its treasures carried in triumph. Back home he ran his father's guard and did his dirty work. People feared he would be another Nero, and his love affair with the Jewish queen Berenice scandalised Rome.

As emperor he surprised them. He sent Berenice away, stopped treason trials and handed out favours freely. Then came the disasters. In 79 Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. In 80 a fire raged in Rome for three days, and there was a plague. That same year he opened the Colosseum with 100 days of games. In September 81 he caught a fever and died, aged 41. His younger brother Domitian took over.

claims.text: Vesuvius erupted on 24 August 79.
claims.note: That date comes from manuscripts of Pliny the Younger's letters. A charcoal inscription found at Pompeii in 2018 points to October instead.

claims.text: Domitian hurried his brother's death along.
claims.note: Suetonius and Cassius Dio hint at it; Dio says Domitian had him packed in snow while still alive. Both writers loathed Domitian.

claims.text: A gnat flew up Titus's nose and gnawed at his brain for seven years as punishment for destroying the Temple.
claims.note: A Jewish tradition preserved in the Talmud, told as divine justice, not history.

reigns.hook: Titus dies loved and mourned. His brother Domitian has waited years in his shadow. He has no intention of sharing power with anyone, least of all the Senate.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who wanted to be called lord and god
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by the Guard when Titus died
reigns.previously: Titus, the people's favourite, died of a fever after two years.
paragraphs: Domitian ruled for 15 years, longer than anyone since Tiberius, and he worked hard. He rebuilt Rome after the fire of 80, put up a vast palace on the Palatine and a stadium whose outline is now the Piazza Navona. He improved the silver coinage and gave the army a pay rise of a third. He fought the Chatti in Germany and the Dacians on the Danube, where one of his armies was wiped out. Peace with Dacia came at a price.

In 89 a governor in Germany, Saturninus, rebelled. It failed, but Domitian grew suspicious and cruel. Senators were executed and philosophers thrown out of Rome. He liked to be called 'lord and god'. The senators who wrote his history hated him. On 18 September 96 a steward called Stephanus, his arm in a bandage hiding a dagger, stabbed him in his rooms. The Senate cursed his memory that same day and named an old senator, Nerva, as emperor.

claims.text: He demanded to be addressed as 'dominus et deus', lord and god.
claims.note: Suetonius says so, and court poets like Martial used the phrase, but it never appears on his official coins or inscriptions.

claims.text: He spent hours alone stabbing flies with a pen.
claims.note: Suetonius tells it, and Dio has a courtier joke that not even a fly was with the emperor. A great story with a hostile source.

claims.text: His wife Domitia was in on the plot.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says she knew. Yet for decades afterwards she proudly called herself Domitian's wife.

reigns.hook: Domitian's body is barely cold and the Senate is already chiselling his name off monuments. Their pick for emperor is an elderly lawyer with no children.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap emperor who picked a winner
reigns.previously: Domitian was stabbed in his palace. The Senate cursed his memory.
paragraphs: Nerva was a lawyer and a survivor. He had done well under Nero, Vespasian and Domitian alike, and he was 65, childless and in poor health. That made him perfect: a safe pair of hands who wouldn't last long. He freed Domitian's political prisoners, called back exiles, cut taxes and swore no senator would be put to death. Rome breathed out.

The army had loved Domitian, though. In 97 the Praetorian Guard besieged the palace and forced Nerva to hand over Domitian's killers, whom they butchered. He even had to thank the Guard in public. Humiliated, he made a smart move. He adopted Trajan, a respected general commanding on the Rhine. With a strong heir in place, nobody dared push Nerva around. He died of a fever in January 98, the first of the 'Five Good Emperors'.

claims.text: He swore that no senator would be put to death while he ruled, and kept his word.
claims.note: Cassius Dio reports the oath, and no senator is known to have been executed in his short reign.

claims.text: When the Guard rioted, Nerva bared his throat and offered to die rather than give up the assassins.
claims.note: Only a short late summary, the Epitome de Caesaribus, tells it; in the end he gave way anyway.

claims.text: He announced Trajan's adoption with a line from Homer: 'May the Greeks pay for my tears with your arrows.'
claims.note: It survives only in a Byzantine summary of Cassius Dio's history.

reigns.hook: Nerva is dead after sixteen months. His heir is far off on the Rhine and in no hurry to come home. Trajan, the soldier from Spain, is going to make the empire bigger than ever.

reigns.tagline: The best of emperors, and the biggest empire
reigns.reignEnded: Stroke on the way home from war
reigns.previously: Nerva, bullied by the Guard, adopted the general Trajan and died.
paragraphs: Trajan was the first emperor born outside Italy, at Italica in southern Spain. He took his time coming to Rome and, when he did, walked in on foot among the crowds. The Senate adored him and eventually gave him the title Optimus, 'the best'. He fought two wars against Decebalus of Dacia, in modern Romania. Decebalus killed himself, Dacia became a province, and its gold paid for a grand new forum and market in Rome.

Trajan's Column still stands there, with a spiral frieze telling the Dacian wars in pictures. In 114 he went east against Parthia, took Armenia and Mesopotamia and reached the Persian Gulf. The empire was now at its largest ever. Then revolts broke out behind him and his health failed. He suffered a stroke and died at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117. His ashes were placed in the base of his Column.

claims.text: At the Persian Gulf he watched a ship sail for India and wished he were young enough to follow Alexander.
claims.note: A touching scene from Cassius Dio, written about a century later. Nobody else records it.

claims.text: Later senators hailed each new emperor with 'luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan'.
claims.note: The historian Eutropius, writing in the late 300s, says the Senate still used the cheer in his own day.

claims.text: His ashes were buried inside the base of Trajan's Column.
claims.note: Cassius Dio and Eutropius both say so, and the chamber survives, though the golden urn is long gone.

reigns.hook: Trajan is dead in a small town in Asia Minor. Days later a letter says he adopted his cousin's son Hadrian on his deathbed. The letter is signed by his widow.

reigns.tagline: The restless emperor who drew a line across Britain
reigns.previously: Trajan died in Cilicia, with the empire at its biggest ever.
paragraphs: Hadrian started by giving up Trajan's new conquests in the East, which he thought could not be held. Four leading senators were executed in his first year, and the Senate never forgave him. He then spent more than half his reign on the road, inspecting armies and cities. In Britain in 122 he ordered a wall from the Tyne to the Solway, about 73 miles long. He loved all things Greek and was the first emperor to wear a full beard.

He rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome, which still stands with its great dome, and built a huge villa at Tivoli. His beloved young companion Antinous drowned in the Nile in 130; Hadrian founded a city in his name and had him worshipped as a god. A Jewish revolt in Judaea from 132 to 135 was crushed with terrible bloodshed. His first choice of heir died, so in 138 he adopted Antoninus, on condition that Antoninus adopt young Marcus Aurelius.

claims.text: Trajan never adopted Hadrian; the empress Plotina faked it.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says the adoption was announced only after Trajan died, and that Plotina signed the letter. Dio had his story from his father.

claims.text: Antinous didn't fall into the Nile by accident. He was sacrificed or gave his life for Hadrian.
claims.note: Hadrian himself called it an accident. Cassius Dio thought it was a sacrifice. Nobody really knows.

claims.text: He grew his beard to hide blemishes on his face.
claims.note: This comes from the Historia Augusta, a late collection of biographies notorious for gossip and invention.

reigns.hook: Hadrian dies by the sea, writing a little poem to his own soul. His heir is a mild, wealthy senator of 51, already lined up to hand the throne to young Marcus.

reigns.tagline: Twenty-three quiet years, and that was the point
reigns.previously: Hadrian died at Baiae after naming Antoninus as his heir.
paragraphs: Antoninus was rich, kindly and careful with money. He began by forcing a reluctant Senate to make Hadrian a god, which may be how he earned the name Pius, 'dutiful'. He then ruled for 23 years with hardly a crisis. He seems never to have left Italy, running the empire by letter. In Britain his generals pushed north and built a second barrier, the turf Antonine Wall between the Forth and the Clyde. It was given up after about 20 years.

When his wife Faustina died in 140 he made her a goddess and set up a charity for poor girls in her name. Their temple still stands in the Roman Forum. He married his daughter to Marcus Aurelius and trained Marcus for years in the business of ruling. When he died at his country estate in March 161, aged 74, he left a full treasury and an empire at peace. Historians find his reign almost boringly calm.

claims.text: He was called Pius because he bullied the Senate into deifying Hadrian.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta offers several other explanations too, like helping his elderly father-in-law. This is the one most historians favour.

claims.text: He never left Italy in all his 23 years as emperor.
claims.note: No good evidence puts him abroad, and the ancient sources stress how much he stayed home. Silence isn't proof.

claims.text: After eating too much Alpine cheese, he gave the guard the password 'Equanimity', turned over and died.
claims.note: It's from the Historia Augusta, which is unreliable, though this part may come from a better lost source.

reigns.hook: Antoninus dies calm as ever. Marcus Aurelius is the heir, but he does something no emperor has done before: he insists on sharing the throne with his adoptive brother Lucius.

reigns.title: Marcus Aurelius & Lucius Verus
reigns.tagline: Rome's first double act, hit by war and plague
reigns.previously: Antoninus Pius dies in his bed after 23 calm years.
paragraphs: Hadrian had planned this years ahead: Antoninus adopted both young men. When the old emperor died, the Senate offered Marcus the throne alone. He refused unless his adoptive brother Lucius got exactly the same title. Rome had never had two emperors at once. They made an odd pair. Marcus was serious and bookish. Lucius loved chariot racing, parties and good food.

Trouble came at once. Parthia invaded Armenia and wiped out a Roman army, so Lucius went east in 162. His generals, above all Avidius Cassius, did the hard fighting and burned the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon, in 165. Lucius married Marcus's daughter Lucilla. But the returning troops brought home a plague, probably smallpox, which killed huge numbers across the empire.

Then Germanic tribes pushed across the Danube. In 168 both emperors went north together. Heading back to Rome early in 169, Lucius collapsed in his carriage near Altinum and died a few days later. Marcus brought the body home, gave him a lavish funeral and had him declared a god.

claims.text: Marcus poisoned Lucius with a knife smeared with poison on one side only.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta repeats this as gossip, and it's notoriously unreliable. Cassius Dio mentions poison rumours too, but no good evidence backs them.

claims.text: The plague was released when Roman soldiers opened a sealed chest in a temple at Seleucia.
claims.note: Told by Ammianus Marcellinus two centuries later. It reads as a tale of divine punishment.

claims.text: The Antonine Plague was smallpox.
claims.note: The doctor Galen saw it and described a black rash and fever. Most historians think that fits smallpox, but it can't be proved.

reigns.hook: Lucius is dead and the northern frontier is on fire. Marcus, a man who'd rather be reading philosophy, must now run the empire and its wars alone.

reigns.title: Marcus Aurelius, alone
reigns.tagline: The philosopher emperor stuck in a war he never wanted
reigns.reignEnded: Died on campaign by the Danube
reigns.previously: Lucius Verus collapses on the road home and dies. Marcus rules alone.
paragraphs: Marcus spent most of the 170s in army camps along the Danube, fighting the Marcomanni, Quadi and Sarmatians. Money was so tight that he auctioned off palace treasures to pay for the war. At night, in his tent, he wrote notes to himself in Greek about duty, death and keeping calm. We call them the Meditations, and people still buy them by the million.

In 175 a false rumour said Marcus was dead. Avidius Cassius, the hero of the Parthian war, declared himself emperor in the East. Within three months one of his own officers killed him. Marcus is said to have burned Cassius's letters unread so he wouldn't have to punish anyone. His wife Faustina died in the East soon afterwards.

For almost a century emperors had picked their heirs by adoption. Marcus had a son, and in 177 he made Commodus his co-emperor. In March 180, ill and worn out on the frontier, Marcus died. The war was still unfinished.

claims.text: A sudden thunderstorm saved a Roman army trapped and dying of thirst, the so-called Rain Miracle.
claims.note: The storm appears on the Column of Marcus Aurelius. Dio credits an Egyptian magician; Christian writers credited the prayers of Christian soldiers.

claims.text: Faustina encouraged Avidius Cassius to rebel, believing Marcus was dying.
claims.note: Cassius Dio reports it. It may be hostile gossip, and Marcus himself never blamed her in public.

claims.text: The Meditations were never meant to be read by anyone else.
claims.note: The manuscripts call the work 'To Himself', and it reads as a private notebook. How it survived is unknown.

reigns.hook: The wisest man in Rome leaves the empire to his 18-year-old son. Commodus doesn't care for philosophy. He'd much rather be in the arena.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who fought as a gladiator, and always won
reigns.reignEnded: Strangled in his bath by a wrestler
reigns.previously: Marcus Aurelius dies on the Danube. His son Commodus inherits.
paragraphs: Commodus made peace with the northern tribes and hurried home to Rome. In 182 his sister Lucilla plotted to kill him. The assassin pulled a dagger and shouted that the Senate had sent it, which gave the game away before he struck. After that Commodus trusted almost nobody but his favourites. The prefect Perennis ran things until 185, then the freedman Cleander, who sold offices to the highest bidder.

When a grain shortage hit Rome in 190, a furious crowd demanded Cleander's head, and Commodus handed it over. By now he thought he was Hercules. He wore a lion skin, renamed Rome after himself and fought in the arena, killing animals by the hundred and taking on gladiators who knew better than to win.

His mistress Marcia, his chamberlain Eclectus and the guard prefect Laetus decided he had to go. On the last night of 192 Marcia gave him poisoned food. He vomited it up, so they sent in his wrestling partner, Narcissus, who strangled him in the bath.

claims.text: In the arena he cut off an ostrich's head and waved it at the senators, grinning.
claims.note: Cassius Dio was in the seats. He says he chewed laurel leaves from his wreath to stop himself laughing.

claims.text: Commodus was really the son of a gladiator, not of Marcus Aurelius.
claims.note: Gossip about his mother Faustina in the Historia Augusta, a notoriously unreliable source.

claims.text: He planned to start 193 as consul, walking out of the gladiators' barracks.
claims.note: Dio and Herodian both report it as the last straw. It may also be what the plotters said to justify themselves.

reigns.hook: New Year's Day, 193. The palace has a corpse and no heir. The killers need a respected old senator to put their name to, and fast.

reigns.tagline: The honest old soldier who lasted 87 days
reigns.previously: Commodus is strangled in his bath on the last night of 192.
paragraphs: Pertinax was the son of a freed slave from northern Italy. He started out as a schoolteacher, joined the army and climbed all the way to consul under Marcus Aurelius. When Laetus came knocking on the night Commodus died, he was 66 and in charge of the city of Rome. He went to the Praetorian camp, promised the guards a bonus, and the Senate gladly accepted him.

He found the treasury nearly empty. So he auctioned off Commodus's things, from his silk robes to his chariots, and tried to bring back discipline. The guards hated that. On 28 March about 300 of them marched into the palace. Pertinax went out and tried to talk them down. One soldier speared him, and the rest finished him off. His head went back to the camp on a spear.

claims.text: Pertinax sold off Commodus's possessions at a public auction to pay the bills.
claims.note: Cassius Dio, a senator in Rome at the time, describes the sale.

claims.text: When Laetus arrived at night, Pertinax assumed he'd been sent to kill him.
claims.note: Dio and Herodian tell versions of the scene; it makes a neat story and may be polished.

reigns.hook: The guards have murdered their emperor and the throne is empty. Now they have a shocking idea: sell it to whoever pays the most.

reigns.tagline: The man who bought the Roman Empire at auction
reigns.cameToPower: Won an auction for the throne
reigns.reignEnded: Killed in the palace after 66 days
reigns.previously: Pertinax is killed by his own guards after 87 days.
paragraphs: After killing Pertinax, the guards shut themselves in their camp and took bids. Inside, Pertinax's father-in-law, Sulpicianus, made offers. Outside, a wealthy senator named Didius Julianus shouted his bids up at the wall. He won by promising each guard 25,000 sesterces. They marched him to the Senate, which had no choice. The people of Rome jeered and threw stones at him.

Three armies soon named their own emperors: Septimius Severus on the Danube, Pescennius Niger in Syria and Clodius Albinus in Britain. Severus was closest and came straight for Italy. Julianus tried to fortify Rome and even offered to share power. It was hopeless. The Senate switched sides, condemned him to death and sent a soldier to the palace to kill him.

claims.text: The guards sold the empire to the highest bidder.
claims.note: Cassius Dio, who was in Rome, describes the auction in detail, and Herodian agrees.

claims.text: His last words were: 'But what evil have I done? Whom have I killed?'
claims.note: Reported by Cassius Dio. He hadn't been in the room, but he was in Rome that day.

reigns.hook: Severus enters Rome at the head of his legions. But two more generals claim the purple, and one of them holds the entire East.

reigns.tagline: The African general who ran Rome like an army camp
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; governor on the Danube
reigns.previously: Julianus has bought the throne. Generals revolt across the empire.
paragraphs: Severus came from Leptis Magna in North Africa. He reached Rome in June 193 and sacked the entire Praetorian Guard, replacing it with his own legionaries. To keep Clodius Albinus quiet he named him his heir, then beat Niger in the East in 194. With Niger dead, he turned on Albinus and crushed him near Lyon in 197 in one of the biggest battles Romans ever fought against Romans. Dozens of senators who had backed Albinus were executed.

Then he sacked the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon, and added a new province, Mesopotamia. He raised army pay and let soldiers marry. His Syrian wife, Julia Domna, was clever and powerful. In 208 he took his two quarrelling sons to Britain to fight in Scotland, partly to toughen them up. He died at York in February 211.

claims.text: On his deathbed he told his sons: 'Get along, make the soldiers rich, and ignore everyone else.'
claims.note: Cassius Dio reports it. Dio knew Severus but wasn't at the deathbed.

claims.text: In Scotland, Caracalla drew his sword to stab his father in the back.
claims.note: Only Dio tells the story; it may be coloured by his hatred of Caracalla.

claims.text: Severus sent his sister home to Africa because her Latin embarrassed him.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta says so, and it's notoriously unreliable.

reigns.hook: Severus told his sons to get along. Caracalla and Geta can't stand each other. Now they have to share one throne.

reigns.title: Caracalla & Geta
reigns.tagline: Two brothers, one throne, and a mother caught between
reigns.previously: Septimius Severus dies at York, leaving the empire to two sons.
paragraphs: Both brothers already held the title of emperor. They dropped the war in Scotland, made peace and sailed home with their father's ashes, hardly speaking. In Rome they split the palace in two, blocked the connecting doors and kept separate guards. Each was terrified the other would poison him.

In December Caracalla asked to meet Geta in their mother's rooms to make peace. When Geta arrived, centurions burst in and cut him down. He died clinging to Julia Domna, whose hand was wounded trying to protect him. Caracalla rushed to the army camp, claimed Geta had plotted against him and handed out cash. Then came a purge of Geta's friends and supporters, and Geta's face was chiselled off monuments.

claims.text: Geta died in his mother's arms.
claims.note: Cassius Dio, a senator at the time, gives the details, including Julia Domna's wounded hand.

claims.text: The brothers planned to split the empire, East and West, until their mother asked how they would divide her.
claims.note: Only Herodian tells it, and he loves a dramatic speech.

claims.text: Some 20,000 people were killed in the purge after Geta's death.
claims.note: The figure is Dio's. It's probably exaggerated, though the purge was real.

reigns.hook: Geta is dead and his name is being scratched off every monument. Caracalla has the empire to himself, and an army whose love he means to buy.

reigns.title: Caracalla, alone
reigns.tagline: The brother-killer who made everyone a Roman
reigns.previously: Caracalla has his brother Geta killed in their mother's arms.
paragraphs: His real name was Antoninus. 'Caracalla' was a nickname from the long hooded Gallic cloak he wore. In 212 he gave Roman citizenship to almost every free person in the empire. He raised army pay steeply and built the vast Baths of Caracalla, whose ruins still tower over Rome. He worshipped Alexander the Great and even formed a phalanx of soldiers armed like Macedonians.

He spent his reign on the move, fighting on the Rhine, then heading east. In 215 he ordered a massacre of young men in Alexandria. Next he wanted a war with Parthia. On 8 April 217, riding from Edessa to Carrhae, he stopped by the road to relieve himself. A soldier named Julius Martialis ran up and stabbed him. The man behind it was his own prefect, Macrinus.

claims.text: He handed out citizenship mainly to collect more tax.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says so, since new citizens paid inheritance tax. Dio loathed Caracalla, so he may be unfair.

claims.text: He ordered a massacre in Alexandria in 215.
claims.note: Both contemporary historians, Dio and Herodian, report it, though they differ on why and on how many died.

claims.text: Martialis killed him over a personal grudge.
claims.note: Dio says Caracalla had refused him a promotion; Herodian says his brother had been executed. Either way Macrinus used him.

reigns.hook: Caracalla lies dead on a desert road. Nobody suspects the grieving prefect who arranges the funeral. Within days, Macrinus is emperor.

reigns.tagline: The first emperor who had never sat in the Senate
reigns.previously: Caracalla is stabbed on the road to Carrhae.
paragraphs: Macrinus came from Caesarea in Mauretania, in North Africa. He was a lawyer and administrator, not a senator, and no one like him had worn the purple before. He made his young son Diadumenian his heir. He fought the Parthians to a draw at Nisibis, then paid a fortune for peace. When he cut pay for new recruits, the army began to grumble.

Caracalla's mother, Julia Domna, died soon after her son. Her sister, Julia Maesa, went home to Emesa in Syria with a fortune and two grandsons. The elder, a 14-year-old priest of the sun god Elagabal, was put about as Caracalla's secret son. In May 218 a nearby legion hailed him emperor. Macrinus lost a battle outside Antioch and fled in disguise. He was caught at Chalcedon and executed, and his son was killed too.

claims.text: Macrinus arranged Caracalla's murder.
claims.note: Dio and Herodian both say so. He seems to have feared Caracalla was about to have him killed.

claims.text: The boy priest of Emesa was Caracalla's son.
claims.note: His grandmother Julia Maesa spread the story to win over the troops, who had loved Caracalla.

claims.text: He shaved his head and beard to escape in disguise.
claims.note: Reported by Cassius Dio. Plausible, but it's the kind of detail a hostile writer enjoys.

reigns.hook: The East has a new emperor: a 14-year-old sun priest in silk robes and eye make-up. Rome has no idea what is heading its way.

reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by a legion in Syria
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by guards, thrown in the Tiber
reigns.previously: Macrinus is beaten outside Antioch and hunted down.
paragraphs: His family called him Varius Avitus Bassianus. As emperor he took Caracalla's official name, but Rome nicknamed him after his god, Elagabal. He brought the god's sacred black stone from Emesa, built it a temple on the Palatine Hill and ranked it above Jupiter. He married a Vestal Virgin, which horrified traditional Romans, and went through several wives in four years.

He danced at the altar in Eastern robes and wore make-up, and the senators were appalled. His grandmother Julia Maesa saw the danger and made him adopt his 12-year-old cousin, Alexander, as his heir. Elagabalus soon regretted it and tried to get rid of the boy. The guards, who liked Alexander, mutinied in March 222. They killed Elagabalus and his mother, Julia Soaemias, and threw his body into the Tiber.

claims.text: He smothered dinner guests to death under a shower of rose petals.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta tells it, and it's notoriously unreliable. Alma-Tadema's 1888 painting made the story famous.

claims.text: He married a Vestal Virgin, Aquilia Severa.
claims.note: Cassius Dio reports it, and coins were struck in her name as empress.

claims.text: He called himself the wife of his charioteer, Hierocles.
claims.note: Reported by Cassius Dio, who was hostile and wrote soon afterwards. Hard to separate fact from slander.

reigns.hook: The guards have a new emperor: Elagabalus's 13-year-old cousin. The real power stands right behind him. It's his mother.

reigns.tagline: A mother's boy in an age that wanted a soldier
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Cousin and adopted son of Elagabalus
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by his troops near Mainz
reigns.previously: Elagabalus and his mother are killed and thrown into the Tiber.
paragraphs: Alexander was a polite, earnest boy, and the women of his family ran his government. First his grandmother Julia Maesa, then his mother, Julia Mamaea. The Senate was treated with respect again. But the guards were hard to control. They murdered the great lawyer Ulpian, their own prefect, in the palace. Mamaea even drove out Alexander's wife when she grew too popular.

Then the world changed. In Persia a new dynasty, the Sasanians, overthrew the Parthians and attacked Roman Mesopotamia. Alexander's eastern campaign in the early 230s ended in a costly draw. Next the Germans crossed the Rhine. At Mainz, Alexander tried to buy peace. His soldiers were disgusted. In March 235 they hailed a giant officer from Thrace, Maximinus, and killed Alexander and his mother in their tent.

claims.text: He kept a private shrine with statues of Abraham, Christ, Orpheus and Apollonius.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta says so, and it's notoriously unreliable.

claims.text: Julia Mamaea summoned the Christian thinker Origen to teach her.
claims.note: Reported by the church historian Eusebius about a century later. Plausible, but no other source confirms it.

claims.text: He died clinging to his mother and blaming her for his fate.
claims.note: Herodian, writing soon after, tells it this way. It fits his picture of a weak boy ruled by his mother.

reigns.hook: The Severans are finished. The army's new emperor is a huge Thracian soldier who will never set foot in Rome. Half a century of chaos is starting.

reigns.tagline: The giant soldier who never set foot in Rome as emperor
reigns.relationToPredecessor: None; a career soldier from Thrace
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by the army on the Rhine
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by his troops at Aquileia
reigns.previously: Severus Alexander and his mother are killed by their own soldiers.
paragraphs: Maximinus came from the rough frontier country of Thrace and climbed the army ladder on sheer muscle. In March 235 the troops on the Rhine got sick of young Severus Alexander and his mother, killed them both, and hailed Maximinus instead. He was the first emperor to rise from the ranks as a common soldier. The senators in Rome were horrified. He never once came to see them.

He spent his whole reign at war. He pushed deep into Germany, and archaeologists have found a battlefield from these years at Harzhorn in Lower Saxony, littered with Roman arrowheads and kit. Then he fought on the Danube. Wars cost money, and his agents squeezed cities, temples and the rich without mercy. In early 238 a group of young landowners in Africa snapped. They killed his tax official and made their own emperor.

The Senate backed the rebels and declared Maximinus a public enemy. He marched on Italy, but the city of Aquileia shut its gates and held out. His army was stuck outside the walls, short of food and miserable. In the spring of 238 his own soldiers turned on him and cut him down in his tent, along with his son Maximus. Their heads were sent to Rome.

claims.text: Maximinus was a giant over eight feet tall who wore his wife's bracelet as a ring on his thumb.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta, a notoriously unreliable late source that loves a tall tale. Herodian calls him huge but gives no such figures.

claims.text: He never visited Rome during his reign.
claims.note: Herodian, who lived through these years, makes a point of it, and nothing contradicts him.

claims.text: He started life as a shepherd boy.
claims.note: Herodian says so, but he wanted to paint Maximinus as a low-born brute. Some historians think his family was more comfortable than that.

reigns.hook: Out in Africa, a mob of angry landowners has just thrust a purple robe on the province's elderly governor, Gordian. He's nearly 80. The Senate is about to bet everything on him.

reigns.title: Gordian I & Gordian II
reigns.tagline: Emperor at nearly 80, and dead three weeks later
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Governor of Africa and his son
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed by tax rebels in Africa
reigns.reignEnded: Son killed in battle; father hanged
reigns.previously: Maximinus's tax men squeeze the provinces until Africa snaps.
paragraphs: Early in 238 young landowners near Thysdrus, in the province of Africa, had had enough of Maximinus's tax collector. They murdered him, and then needed a leader before Maximinus came for them. They picked the provincial governor, Gordian, a rich senator of nearly 80. He made his son, also called Gordian, his co-emperor and moved into Carthage.

In Rome the Senate jumped at the chance. It recognised the Gordians, declared Maximinus a public enemy, and had his praetorian prefect in the city killed. Provinces began to come over. But next door in Numidia sat Capelianus, who commanded the only legion in the region and had an old feud with Gordian. He stayed loyal to Maximinus and marched on Carthage.

Gordian II led out a big crowd of townsmen who had never fought. Capelianus's veterans cut them to pieces outside Carthage, and the young emperor died with them. When the news reached his father, the old man hanged himself with his belt. They had lasted about three weeks. The Senate was now at war with Maximinus, with no emperor of its own.

claims.text: Gordian I and II ruled for only about 20 days.
claims.note: Herodian and later writers agree it was a matter of weeks. When those weeks fell is argued: March to April is traditional, some say January.

claims.text: Gordian I was descended from the Gracchi brothers on one side and the emperor Trajan on the other.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta says so, and this grand family tree looks like one of its many inventions.

claims.text: Gordian II kept 22 concubines and a library of 62,000 books.
claims.note: Both figures come from the Historia Augusta, which loves a big number and is notoriously unreliable.

reigns.hook: Both Gordians are dead and Maximinus is coming. The Senate has gone too far to back down. Behind closed doors, the senators choose two emperors from their own ranks.

reigns.title: Pupienus & Balbinus
reigns.tagline: Two old senators, one throne and a guard with a grudge
reigns.previously: Gordian II dies in battle and his father hangs himself at Carthage.
paragraphs: The Senate picked two of its own: Pupienus, a hard old general who had been prefect of the city, and Balbinus, a rich aristocrat from an old family. The Roman crowd hated the choice and blocked their way with stones and sticks. It wanted a Gordian. So the senators fetched the dead man's grandson, a boy of 13, and made him Caesar, the junior emperor. The crowd went home.

Pupienus marched north to face Maximinus, but he never had to fight him. Maximinus was stuck outside Aquileia, which shut its gates and held out. His hungry, fed-up soldiers killed him and his son in their tent and sent the heads to Rome. Back in the city, meanwhile, the Praetorian Guard and the mob had fought in the streets, and whole districts burned.

Victory should have saved them. It didn't. Pupienus came home with a German bodyguard, and the Praetorians saw insult everywhere. The two emperors couldn't stand each other either. On 29 July 238 the guards burst into the palace while the old men were quarrelling, dragged them through the streets, tortured them and killed them. Then they hailed the only emperor left: the boy, Gordian III.

claims.text: The guards caught Pupienus and Balbinus arguing, each suspecting the other of plotting.
claims.note: Herodian, writing within living memory, describes the quarrel that left them helpless when the guards broke in.

claims.text: Maximinus was killed outside Aquileia in May 238.
claims.note: Herodian gives no dates. Modern estimates run from April to June, tied up with the argument over when the Gordians rose.

claims.text: Pupienus was the son of a blacksmith.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta says a blacksmith or a cartwright, which sounds like guesswork. It is notoriously unreliable.

reigns.hook: A 13-year-old now sits on the throne, put there by the men who just murdered his colleagues. Someone grown-up will have to run things, and plenty of people want the job.

reigns.tagline: The teenage emperor who never came home from Persia
reigns.previously: The Praetorian Guard murders Pupienus and Balbinus in the palace.
paragraphs: Gordian III was popular, mostly because he was young and his family had died fighting Maximinus. Real power sat with the people around him. In 241 he married Tranquillina, daughter of Timesitheus, a sharp administrator who became Praetorian Prefect and effectively ran the empire. By most accounts he ran it well.

Trouble was building in the East. Persia had a new and very aggressive dynasty, the Sasanians, and their king Shapur I had his eye on Rome's eastern provinces. In 242 Gordian and Timesitheus set out with a big army. They won a battle at Resaena in 243 and pushed the Persians back. Then Timesitheus fell ill and died. His replacement as prefect was an ambitious officer called Philip.

Early in 244 the army was deep in Mesopotamia when Gordian died, aged 19. How he died is one of the great mysteries of the age. Shapur boasted that he beat and killed him in battle. Roman writers said Philip turned the hungry troops against him. Either way, Philip was the man who came out of it wearing purple.

claims.text: Gordian was killed in a great battle against Shapur at Misiche.
claims.note: Shapur's own victory inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam says so. Roman sources never mention a defeat, which is partly why some historians believe it.

claims.text: Philip had him murdered.
claims.note: Later Roman writers such as Zosimus and the Historia Augusta blame Philip, but they wrote long afterwards, and the Historia Augusta is notoriously unreliable.

claims.text: His soldiers raised a monument to him near the Euphrates.
claims.note: Ammianus Marcellinus saw it at Zaitha when he marched past with Julian's army in 363.

reigns.hook: Philip is emperor, stuck in enemy country with an army far from home. He needs peace with Persia, and fast. Shapur knows it, and names his price.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who threw Rome a 1,000th birthday party
reigns.previously: Young Gordian III dies in Mesopotamia, in very murky circumstances.
paragraphs: Philip was born in a small town in what is now southern Syria, the son of a local notable. Ancient writers sneered at his Arab roots, and the nickname stuck. His first job was getting out of Persia alive. He made peace with Shapur and paid him 500,000 denarii, which Shapur happily advertised as tribute. Back home, Philip rebuilt his birthplace as a showy new city and named it Philippopolis after himself.

His big moment came in April 248, when Rome turned 1,000 years old by its own count. Philip threw a huge festival with games, shows and wild beasts in the arena, and coins announced a new age. But the empire was cracking. Goths and Carpi raided across the Danube, and armies in the Balkans and the East kept proclaiming emperors of their own.

Philip sent a respected senator, Decius, to sort out the Danube legions. It worked too well. In 249 the troops there proclaimed Decius emperor. The two armies met near Verona that autumn, and Philip was killed. In Rome, the Praetorian Guard murdered his young son and co-emperor, Philip II.

claims.text: Philip was secretly the first Christian emperor.
claims.note: Eusebius tells a story of him doing penance at Easter before a bishop. Most historians doubt it, since nothing in his public acts looks Christian.

claims.text: Shapur claimed the peace payment as tribute from a beaten Rome.
claims.note: His inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam says so. It's victory propaganda, but historians accept that a large payment was made.

claims.text: Decius took the throne only because the troops threatened to kill him.
claims.note: Zosimus says so. It's a handy story for any usurper, and impossible to check.

reigns.hook: Decius is a proud old Roman who thinks the empire's troubles come from angry gods. His plan to win them back will reach into every household in the empire.

reigns.tagline: He made everyone sacrifice, then died in a Gothic swamp
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Philip's general, who turned on him
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by the Goths at Abritus
reigns.previously: Philip the Arab dies fighting Decius near Verona.
paragraphs: Decius came from near Sirmium in the Balkans, but he loved old Roman tradition. He even added Trajan's name to his own. Soon after taking power he gave an order: everyone in the empire had to sacrifice to the gods in front of officials and get a signed certificate to prove it. He probably saw it as a grand act of loyalty and unity. For Christians it was a nightmare.

Dozens of these certificates have turned up on papyrus in Egypt. Many Christians gave in, some bought fake certificates, and some refused and died. Fabian, the bishop of Rome, was among the victims. The row over what to do with those who caved would split the Church for years.

Then the Goths, led by a king called Cniva, poured across the Danube and sacked Philippopolis in Thrace. Decius went after them. In June 251, at Abritus in what is now Bulgaria, he chased them into marshy ground and was trapped. He and his son Herennius Etruscus were both killed. He was the first Roman emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy.

claims.text: Decius's body was never found because it sank into the swamp.
claims.note: Aurelius Victor and Jordanes say so. It's plausible, but they were writing a century or more later.

claims.text: Trebonianus Gallus betrayed him to the Goths.
claims.note: Zosimus says so, but earlier writers don't, and Gallus may just have been a convenient villain.

claims.text: Signed certificates of sacrifice from his reign still survive.
claims.note: Dozens of these libelli, mostly from Egypt, have been found on papyrus.

reigns.hook: The emperor lies dead in a bog. The beaten army picks one of its generals, Trebonianus Gallus, who now has to deal with the Goths and something far deadlier.

reigns.previously: Decius and his son die fighting the Goths at Abritus.
paragraphs: Gallus needed the Goths gone, so he let them leave with their loot and their prisoners, and agreed to pay them to stay away. It looked shameful, and people never forgot it. To keep things smooth he adopted Decius's surviving son Hostilian and made him co-emperor. Hostilian died within months, and Gallus raised his own son Volusianus in his place.

The real killer was invisible. A terrible epidemic, now called the Plague of Cyprian after the bishop of Carthage who described it, was spreading across the empire. Cyprian wrote of burning fevers, blood-red eyes and failing limbs. Meanwhile Shapur of Persia smashed a Roman army in the East and sacked Antioch, one of the greatest cities in the empire.

In 253 the governor of Moesia, Aemilian, beat a Gothic raid, and his delighted troops proclaimed him emperor. He marched on Italy. Gallus and Volusianus went to meet him, but at Interamna, north of Rome, their own soldiers decided Aemilian was the better bet and killed them both. Aemilian lasted about three months before his men murdered him too.

claims.text: Young Hostilian died of the plague.
claims.note: Aurelius Victor says plague. Zosimus says Gallus had him killed. The plague version is more widely accepted.

claims.text: Pagans blamed the Christians for the plague and the other disasters.
claims.note: Cyprian wrote a whole tract, To Demetrianus, answering exactly that charge.

claims.text: Gallus had arranged Decius's defeat at Abritus.
claims.note: Only Zosimus says so, long after the event. Most historians are sceptical.

reigns.hook: Aemilian's men turned on him because another army was already on its way. It belongs to Valerian, an old senator with a grown-up son, who means to found a dynasty.

reigns.title: Valerian & Gallienus
reigns.tagline: The emperor who ended his days a Persian prisoner
reigns.cameToPower: Army in the Alps hailed Valerian
reigns.previously: Gallus is killed by his own men, then so is his rival Aemilian.
paragraphs: Valerian was a senior senator in his fifties, sent by Gallus to fetch troops from the Alpine provinces. When Gallus died, those troops proclaimed Valerian instead. He quickly made his grown son Gallienus co-emperor. The empire had too many fires for one man, so they split the work: Gallienus took the West and the Rhine, and Valerian headed East to face Persia.

Things kept going badly. Goths raided by sea along the coasts of the Black Sea. The plague came back. Valerian blamed the Christians and, in 257 and 258, launched a fresh persecution aimed at bishops and clergy. Cyprian of Carthage was beheaded, and so was the bishop of Rome, Sixtus II, along with his deacons.

In 260 Valerian marched to save the city of Edessa, with an army weakened by plague. Shapur won. Valerian ended up in Persian hands along with much of his army. No Roman emperor had ever been taken alive by a foreign enemy. Shapur had the moment carved into the cliffs at Naqsh-e Rustam, among the tombs of the ancient Persian kings, and Valerian died a prisoner.

claims.text: Shapur used Valerian as a footstool to climb onto his horse.
claims.note: Lactantius tells this some 50 years later. He was a Christian writer keen to show persecutors coming to a bad end.

claims.text: After he died, Valerian was skinned, and his skin was dyed red and hung up in a temple.
claims.note: Also from Lactantius, with the same agenda. No Persian or neutral source mentions it.

claims.text: St Lawrence, one of Sixtus's deacons, was roasted alive on a gridiron.
claims.note: Lawrence really was martyred in 258, but most historians think he was beheaded. The gridiron appears in later accounts.

reigns.hook: Gallienus is now alone, and his father is a captive in Persia. Within months, generals in the West and lords in the East will start carving up what's left.

reigns.title: Gallienus, alone
reigns.tagline: He held the centre while the empire broke into three
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered by his officers at Milan
reigns.previously: Valerian is captured by Shapur, the first emperor taken alive.
paragraphs: Gallienus never tried to rescue his father. He had his hands full. In 260 the Rhine general Postumus rebelled and took Gaul, Britain and Spain. In the East, Odaenathus, a powerful lord of the desert city of Palmyra, beat the Persians and became master of the region in all but name. Gallienus gave him grand titles and let him get on with it. The empire was now in three pieces.

He made the best of it. He built a fast cavalry army based at Milan that could rush to any crisis. He stopped senators commanding legions and gave the jobs to tough professional officers. He ended his father's persecution of the Christians. He loved Greek culture and befriended the philosopher Plotinus. Later Latin writers never forgave him, and painted him as a lazy playboy.

In 268 Goths and Heruli rampaged through Greece and sacked Athens. Gallienus beat a big force of them, then rushed back to Italy, where his cavalry commander Aureolus had rebelled at Milan. During the siege of Milan, his own officers plotted against him. One night they raised a false alarm, and when Gallienus ran out without his bodyguard, he was killed.

claims.text: His generals Claudius and Aurelian were in on the plot.
claims.note: Zosimus and other writers implicate Claudius. The Historia Augusta, notoriously unreliable and keen to flatter Claudius as Constantine's supposed ancestor, clears him.

claims.text: Plotinus asked him to found a city run on Plato's laws, to be called Platonopolis.
claims.note: Porphyry, Plotinus's pupil, says so in his Life of Plotinus. Courtiers blocked the plan.

claims.text: Thirty would-be emperors, the 'Thirty Tyrants', rose up against him.
claims.note: The number comes from the Historia Augusta, which pads its list with invented people to echo the Thirty Tyrants of ancient Athens.

reigns.hook: Gallienus is dead, but there's still a second Roman empire in the West. Its founder, Postumus, has been running Gaul, Britain and Spain for eight years as if Rome didn't matter.

reigns.title: The Gallic Empire
reigns.tagline: Gaul, Britain and Spain go it alone for 14 years
reigns.cameToPower: Troops hailed him on the Rhine
reigns.previously: Gallienus is murdered by his own officers outside Milan.
paragraphs: It began in 260 with a row over loot. Postumus, the general on the Rhine, beat a band of raiders and shared the plunder with his men. Gallienus's young son Saloninus, left in charge at Cologne, demanded it back. The troops rebelled, besieged Cologne and killed Saloninus. Postumus became emperor of the West: Gaul, the German frontier, Britain and Spain.

Postumus never marched on Rome. He set up his own empire with its own consuls, its own Praetorian Guard and its own excellent coins, and he defended the Rhine better than Rome had. Gallienus attacked him once and was wounded by an arrow. In 269 Postumus crushed a rival at Mainz but refused to let his soldiers sack the city. Furious, they killed him.

A string of short reigns followed. A soldier called Marius lasted only weeks. Victorinus was murdered in 271. Tetricus, a governor backed by Victorinus's mother Victoria, took over. Spain had already drifted back to Rome. In 274 the emperor Aurelian invaded, and Tetricus lost the decisive battle near Châlons. The breakaway empire was over.

claims.text: Tetricus secretly arranged to lose the battle so he could escape his own soldiers.
claims.note: Aurelius Victor and Eutropius say so. It may be a story to explain why Aurelian later spared him and gave him a job in Italy.

claims.text: Marius had been a blacksmith.
claims.note: Aurelius Victor says he was a metalworker, and the Historia Augusta, as usual, piles colourful details on top.

claims.text: Victorinus was killed by a clerk whose wife he had seduced.
claims.note: Aurelius Victor tells this. It's exactly the kind of gossip ancient writers loved.

reigns.hook: Back in Italy, the new emperor Claudius has no time for Gaul. A vast host of Goths is pouring into the Balkans, and he must meet it head on.

paragraphs: Claudius was a tough Balkan officer, one of the circle around Gallienus at Milan when the emperor was killed. The army chose him to take over, and he finished off the rebel Aureolus. Gallienus's troops were angry about the murder, so Claudius had the Senate declare Gallienus a god. It helped. In late 268 he smashed an invading army of Alamanni near Lake Garda in northern Italy.

His big test came in 269. A huge Gothic force had come down into the Balkans by land and sea. Claudius caught it at Naissus, modern Niš in Serbia, won a crushing victory, then hunted the survivors through the mountains. Thousands of Goths were captured and settled as farmers or drafted into the army. He took the title Gothicus, conqueror of the Goths.

But the plague was still loose, and it got into the army. Early in 270 Claudius caught it and died at Sirmium, after less than two years in power. The Senate loved him, and later writers turned him into a model emperor. His brother Quintillus was proclaimed in Italy, but the army had its own favourite.

claims.text: Constantine the Great was his great-nephew.
claims.note: Constantine's propaganda invented this family link around 310. Historians agree it's a fiction, and it explains why later writers flattered Claudius.

claims.text: He banned soldiers from marrying, so a priest called Valentine married couples in secret.
claims.note: This St Valentine's Day story turns up centuries later. There's no ancient evidence for any such ban.

claims.text: The great victory at Naissus was really won by Gallienus, not Claudius.
claims.note: Zosimus and others credit Claudius in 269, but some historians argue the big Gothic defeat belongs to Gallienus in 268.

reigns.hook: Quintillus lasts a matter of weeks. The army wants the cavalry general Aurelian, a hard man about to take on Goths, Gauls and a desert queen.

reigns.tagline: The hard man who glued a shattered empire back together
reigns.reignEnded: Stabbed by his officers in Thrace
reigns.previously: Claudius Gothicus dies of plague; his brother Quintillus soon follows.
paragraphs: Aurelian was a tough Balkan cavalryman who had risen through the ranks. In 270 the empire was in three pieces, barbarians were raiding Italy, and the money was nearly worthless. He beat the invaders, but they had come close enough to frighten Rome. So he gave the city a new wall, nearly 19 kilometres of brick. Much of it still stands.

Then he went after the breakaways. In 272 he marched east, beat Queen Zenobia's armies and took Palmyra. In 274 he crossed into Gaul and the Gallic Empire folded. He held a huge triumph in Rome, pulled the legions out of Dacia, reformed the coinage and pushed worship of the Unconquered Sun. Coins hailed him as Restorer of the World.

In 275 he set out to fight Persia. Near Byzantium a group of his own officers killed him. The story goes that his secretary, caught lying, forged a death list with their names on it and showed it round.

claims.text: Aurelian's coins called him Restitutor Orbis, the Restorer of the World.
claims.note: The title appears on his surviving coinage, which you can still see in museum collections.

claims.text: A secretary afraid of punishment forged a hit list to get Aurelian killed.
claims.note: Zosimus and the Historia Augusta tell it, with different names for the secretary. The Historia Augusta is notoriously unreliable.

claims.text: Tetricus, the last Gallic emperor, secretly betrayed his own army to Aurelian.
claims.note: Later Latin writers such as Eutropius say so. It may be a tidy explanation for a very quick surrender.

reigns.hook: Aurelian's great victory in the East was over a woman. To see how a widow from the desert came to rule a third of the Roman world, we go back to 270, to Palmyra.
