reigns.title: Zenobia of Palmyra
reigns.tagline: The desert queen who took on Rome and nearly won
reigns.previously: Aurelian is dead, killed by his own officers on the road east.
paragraphs: Palmyra was a rich caravan city in the Syrian desert. Its lord Odaenathus had fought Persia for Rome, and was murdered in 267. His widow Zenobia ruled for their young son Vaballathus. She was clever, ambitious and kept a court of scholars, including the philosopher Longinus.

With Rome distracted, she struck. In 270 her armies took Egypt, then pushed deep into Asia Minor. By 272 her son was calling himself Augustus and her coins called her Augusta. That was a step too far. Aurelian came east, beat her troops at Immae and Emesa, and besieged Palmyra.

Zenobia slipped out heading for Persia and was caught at the Euphrates. Longinus was executed. Palmyra rebelled again in 273 and was sacked. Zenobia was taken to Rome, and what happened to her after that depends on who you believe.

claims.text: Zenobia walked in Aurelian's triumph weighed down by golden chains.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta describes it in loving detail. It's a notoriously unreliable source, though she probably was shown in the triumph.

claims.text: She ended her days in comfort at a villa near Tivoli.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta says so. Zosimus says she died on the journey to Rome.

claims.text: Zenobia claimed descent from Cleopatra.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta reports it. There's no other evidence she said this.

reigns.hook: Aurelian has restored the world and lost his life. The army, ashamed of the murder, asks the Senate to choose an emperor. The Senate picks one of its own, a very old man.

reigns.tagline: The old senator handed a throne nobody wanted
reigns.reignEnded: Died on campaign in Asia Minor
reigns.previously: Zenobia is a prisoner, and Aurelian, her conqueror, is dead.
paragraphs: After Aurelian's murder there was an odd pause. The army, the story goes, sent the choice to the Senate. The Senate politely sent it back. In the end the senators named Marcus Claudius Tacitus, an elderly man of rank. For a moment it looked like the old Senate was back in charge.

It didn't last. Tacitus went east, where Gothic raiders were ravaging Asia Minor, and beat them. Then, in mid 276, he died after a reign of about six months. Some writers say fever; others say his soldiers killed him.
His half-brother Florian, the praetorian prefect, grabbed the throne without asking the Senate. He lasted less than three months. Facing a rival in the East, his own troops murdered him.

claims.text: Tacitus was a descendant of the great historian Tacitus and had his books copied for every library.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta says this, and it invents freely. Most historians don't believe it.

claims.text: Months went by with no emperor while Senate and army each refused to choose.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta and Aurelius Victor describe it. Modern historians think the gap was much shorter.

reigns.hook: Florian's men have killed him. The throne goes to the general they were marching against, a soldier from Sirmium with big plans for the army.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who made his soldiers plant vineyards
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unrelated; a general in the East
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by his troops against Florian
reigns.previously: Old Tacitus dies after six months; Florian is killed by his own men.
paragraphs: Probus came from Sirmium, like Aurelian, and had served under him. He spent his reign rushing from frontier to frontier. He threw Franks and Alamanni back across the Rhine and fought on the Danube. He also crushed a string of would-be emperors, including Saturninus in the East and Proculus and Bonosus in Gaul.
Between wars he put his soldiers to work digging ditches, draining marshes and planting vines, including around his home town. Wine-growing spread along the Rhine and Danube. The troops hated it.
In 282 the legions in Raetia proclaimed his praetorian prefect, Carus. Near Sirmium, Probus's own soldiers turned on him and killed him.

claims.text: Probus said that soon the empire wouldn't need soldiers at all.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta and Aurelius Victor report the remark. It may have been invented to explain why the army killed him.

claims.text: He let provincials plant vines freely, ending old limits on wine-growing.
claims.note: Eutropius and Aurelius Victor both record that he allowed vines in Gaul, Pannonia and elsewhere.

claims.text: He was killed while hiding in an iron watchtower.
claims.note: A detail from the Historia Augusta, which loves a vivid scene.

reigns.hook: Probus is dead and the new emperor is already marching. Carus has two grown sons and his eyes on Persia.

reigns.title: Carus & Carinus
reigns.tagline: A family firm, a Persian war and a bolt from the sky
reigns.previously: Probus is killed by soldiers sick of planting vines.
paragraphs: Carus was Probus's praetorian prefect. In 282 the legions in Raetia hailed him emperor, and within weeks Probus was dead at the hands of his own men. Carus didn't wait for the Senate's blessing; he simply told it what had happened. He made his grown sons, Carinus and Numerian, Caesars, and turned the empire into a family business.

Carinus, the elder, was left to guard the West, and early in 283 his father raised him to Augustus, a full emperor. Carus took young Numerian east. On the way they beat the Sarmatians on the Danube. Then they invaded Persia, whose king, Bahram II, was busy with a rebellion of his own. The Romans marched down the Tigris and took the Persian capital, Ctesiphon.

Carus pushed on beyond the Tigris. In July or August 283, during a violent storm, he died in his tent. Some said lightning hit it. Others said illness, and some modern historians suspect murder. Either way, his two sons were now joint emperors, one at each end of the empire.

claims.text: Carus was killed by a bolt of lightning.
claims.note: Several late Roman writers report it. Others say illness, and some modern historians suspect murder.

claims.text: Fate had decreed that no Roman emperor could go beyond Ctesiphon, and Carus died for trying.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta says people believed this. It reads like an explanation invented after the fact, and later emperors went further.

reigns.hook: Carus is dead in the desert. His sons now share the empire: Carinus in the West, and Numerian with an army deep in Persia that badly wants to go home.

reigns.title: Carinus & Numerian
reigns.tagline: Two brothers, two halves and one very bad smell
reigns.reignEnded: Numerian found dead in his litter
reigns.previously: Carus dies in his tent beyond the Tigris, maybe struck by lightning.
paragraphs: The brothers ruled as joint emperors, Carinus in the West and Numerian with the army in the East. Numerian gave up on Persia and led the army home, back up the Tigris and across Syria and Asia Minor. The real power on the march was his father-in-law, Aper, the praetorian prefect.

On the way Numerian fell ill, with sore eyes it was said, and travelled shut inside a closed litter. Aper passed on his orders. In November 284, near Nicomedia, the soldiers noticed a terrible smell coming from the litter. They pulled back the curtains and found the emperor dead, probably for some days. Aper was the obvious suspect.

The army met outside Nicomedia and chose a commander of the household guard named Diocles. On 20 November 284 he swore before the troops that he had no part in Numerian's death, then drew his sword and killed Aper with his own hand. In the West, Carinus refused to accept him. Their armies met by the river Margus in 285, and Carinus was killed by his own officers.

claims.text: Numerian's death was hidden until his body began to stink.
claims.note: The tale is in Aurelius Victor and the Historia Augusta. The details may be embroidered, but the cover-up is widely accepted.

claims.text: A Druid priestess had told Diocletian he would be emperor once he killed a boar. Aper means "boar".
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta tells it, and it is notoriously unreliable. It's a neat pun, which is a warning sign.

claims.text: Carinus married nine wives, divorcing several while they were pregnant.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta again. Writers loyal to Diocletian had every reason to blacken Carinus's name.

reigns.hook: Diocles takes a grander name, Diocletian. The soldier of humble birth from Dalmatia will soon have the whole empire, and he's going to decide it's too big for one man.

reigns.title: Diocletian & Maximian
reigns.tagline: One empire, four emperors, and a garden of cabbages
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the army at Nicomedia
reigns.reignEnded: Both retired on the same day
reigns.previously: Numerian is found dead in his litter; Aper is killed on the spot.
paragraphs: Diocletian beat Carinus in 285 and then made a big decision: one man couldn't run this empire. He raised his old comrade Maximian, first as Caesar, then in 286 as fellow Augustus in the West. In 293 each took a junior partner, Constantius and Galerius. Four emperors, one system: the Tetrarchy.

It worked. Usurpers were crushed and Persia was beaten. Diocletian rebuilt the army, the provinces and the taxes, and in 301 tried to fix the price of almost everything by law. That failed. From 303 he launched the Great Persecution, the empire's harshest attack on Christians.
Then he did something no emperor had done. On 1 May 305 he stepped down at Nicomedia, and made a reluctant Maximian retire at Milan the same day. Diocletian went home to a vast palace at Split.

claims.text: Asked to come back and sort out the mess, Diocletian said he'd rather show them the cabbages he was growing.
claims.note: The story is in the Epitome de Caesaribus, written decades later. Lovely, but there's no way to check it.

claims.text: Diocletian ordered churches destroyed and scriptures burned from 303.
claims.note: Lactantius and Eusebius lived through it, and the edicts are well documented.

claims.text: His price edict set maximum prices for over a thousand goods and services.
claims.note: Large parts of the edict survive in inscriptions found across the eastern empire.

reigns.hook: Two old men leave the stage. Constantius and Galerius are promoted to Augustus. Constantius's grown son Constantine has been passed over, and he's stuck at Galerius's court.

reigns.title: Constantius I & Galerius
reigns.tagline: Two senior emperors, and a son on the run
reigns.previously: Diocletian and Maximian retire on the same day in 305.
paragraphs: On paper the handover was smooth. Constantius took the West, Galerius the East. But the new junior emperors, Severus and Maximinus Daia, were both Galerius's men. The emperors' grown sons, Constantine and Maxentius, were left out in the cold.

Constantine was at Galerius's court, close to a hostage. He asked to join his sick father, got grudging permission, and left at speed. He caught up with Constantius in Gaul, and they sailed to Britain to fight the Picts.
On 25 July 306 Constantius died at York. His troops didn't wait for Galerius to send word. They hailed his son as emperor on the spot.

claims.text: Constantine escaped by night and killed or maimed the post-horses behind him so no one could follow.
claims.note: Lactantius and later writers tell it. They were Constantine's fans, and the drama may be polish.

claims.text: Constantine's mother Helena was never Constantius's legal wife.
claims.note: Some ancient writers call her a concubine, others a wife. Constantius set her aside to marry Maximian's stepdaughter Theodora.

claims.text: Galerius died of a horrible rotting disease, eaten by worms.
claims.note: Lactantius, a Christian who loathed him, gives the gory details. Galerius did die of a long illness in 311.

reigns.hook: In a fortress at York, soldiers wrap a purple cloak round a young officer. Galerius is furious, but he can't undo it. Constantine is in.

reigns.title: Constantine the Great
reigns.tagline: A sign in the sky, a new faith and a new Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed by the army at York
reigns.previously: Constantius dies at York and his troops hail his son.
paragraphs: Constantine started as one emperor among many. Galerius only grudgingly accepted him, and the West was split with Maxentius in Rome. In 312 Constantine invaded Italy, and on 28 October beat Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. He fought, he said, under the protection of the Christian God.

In 313 he and Licinius agreed to tolerate Christians everywhere. Constantine poured money into churches and in 325 called the Council of Nicaea to settle what Christians believed. He and Licinius fell out twice, and in 324 Constantine won it all. In 326 he had his eldest son Crispus put to death, then his wife Fausta.
He built a new capital on the Bosporus, dedicated in 330 and named after himself: Constantinople. In 337, falling ill near Nicomedia, he was baptised at last and died soon after.

claims.text: Before the Milvian Bridge, Constantine saw a cross of light in the sky with the words “In this sign, conquer”.
claims.note: Eusebius says Constantine told him so years later. Lactantius, writing earlier, mentions only a dream telling him to mark a sign on shields.

claims.text: Fausta was killed in an overheated bath.
claims.note: Later writers say so. Why Crispus and Fausta died was hushed up, and gossip about an affair or false accusation filled the gap.

claims.text: Constantine made Christianity the official religion of the empire.
claims.note: He favoured and funded it, but pagan worship stayed legal. Making it the state religion came under Theodosius.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 306. Three months after York, Rome itself has a new emperor: Maxentius, son of the retired Maximian, and nobody asked Galerius about him either.

paragraphs: Maxentius was the son of one emperor and son-in-law of another, Galerius, yet he was left out in 305. In October 306 Rome was angry about plans to tax the city and cut the Praetorian Guard. The guardsmen hailed Maxentius emperor, and his father Maximian came out of retirement to help.

Severus marched on Rome in 307 and his troops deserted to Maximian. Galerius tried next and had to retreat. Then Maximian tried to rip the purple off his son's shoulders in front of the troops. They sided with Maxentius, and the old man fled to Constantine.
Maxentius held Italy and Africa for six years and built grandly in Rome. In 312 Constantine invaded. Maxentius came out to fight by the Milvian Bridge, was routed, and drowned in the Tiber.

claims.text: Maxentius's head was cut off, carried on a spear through Rome, then sent to Africa.
claims.note: Zosimus and the Latin panegyrics describe the head being shown off in Rome. Sending it on to Africa proved to his old province he was dead.

claims.text: Maxentius was a cruel tyrant who preyed on senators' wives.
claims.note: That picture comes from Eusebius and other writers on the winning side. Some historians see a more ordinary ruler.

reigns.hook: Maxentius is gone and Constantine owns the West. In the East one man is left who can stop him: Licinius, the emperor Galerius made at Carnuntum back in 308.

reigns.tagline: Constantine's brother-in-law, ally and final rival
reigns.previously: Maxentius drowns in the Tiber; Constantine takes Rome.
paragraphs: Licinius was a soldier and an old friend of Galerius. In November 308 the emperors met at Carnuntum on the Danube, with Diocletian called out of retirement to help, and made him Augustus. When Galerius died in 311, Licinius and Maximinus Daia split the East between them.

In 313 he married Constantine's half-sister Constantia at Milan, and the two emperors agreed to tolerate Christians. That spring he crushed Maximinus, who died soon after. Then Licinius had the families of his dead rivals killed, including Galerius's widow and Diocletian's wife.

The brothers-in-law fought in 316 and Licinius lost the Balkans. In 324 they fought again. Constantine won at Adrianople, Crispus won at sea, and Licinius was smashed at Chrysopolis. He surrendered after Constantia begged for his life.

claims.text: Constantine promised to spare Licinius, then had him killed anyway.
claims.note: Ancient writers agree he was executed at Thessalonica in 325. Constantine's side said he was plotting again.

claims.text: Licinius persecuted Christians in his last years.
claims.note: Eusebius says so, but he wrote as Constantine's champion. Licinius did purge Christians from his court.

reigns.hook: Constantine rules alone until 337. Then he dies, and within months soldiers butcher his relatives. Three sons are left standing to share the empire.

reigns.title: Constantine II & Constans
reigns.tagline: Three brothers split the map, and the eldest wants more
reigns.cameToPower: Shared the empire after a purge
reigns.reignEnded: Constantine II killed in an ambush
reigns.previously: Constantine the Great dies in May 337, baptised on his deathbed.
paragraphs: Constantine left a crowded family, and that summer the army thinned it out. Soldiers in Constantinople murdered his two half-brothers and most of their sons, including the Caesar Dalmatius. Only two little boys were spared: Gallus and Julian. On 9 September 337 Constantine's three surviving sons each took the title Augustus.

They carved up the map. Constantine II, the eldest, took Gaul, Britain and Spain. Constans, aged about 14, got Italy, Africa and the Balkans. The middle brother, Constantius II, took the East, where he spent these years fighting Shapur II of Persia. Constantine II saw himself as the senior partner and expected his teenage brother to do as he was told.

Constans soon stopped listening. The two quarrelled over who controlled what, and early in 340 Constantine II marched into Italy while Constans was away in the Balkans. Near Aquileia he rode into an ambush laid by Constans's generals and was cut down. Constans, still only about 17, now ruled the whole West.

claims.text: Constantius II ordered the massacre of his uncles and cousins in 337.
claims.note: Julian, who lost his father in it, blamed Constantius. Eutropius says he allowed it rather than ordered it. The troops may have acted first.

claims.text: Constantine II's body was thrown into the river Alsa near Aquileia.
claims.note: The Epitome de Caesaribus says so, writing about 60 years later. Other accounts just say he was killed near Aquileia.

claims.text: Constantine had been poisoned by his half-brothers and left a note naming them.
claims.note: Only the church historian Philostorgius tells it, about a century later. It looks like a cover story for the killings.

reigns.hook: Constantine II is dead and Constans, still a teenager, rules two-thirds of the empire. In the East his brother Constantius is fighting Persia, and keeping a wary eye on him.

reigns.title: Constans & Constantius II
reigns.tagline: Two brothers, two halves and one fatal birthday party
reigns.previously: Constantine II invades Italy and is killed in an ambush.
paragraphs: Now there were two. Constans ruled the West, from Britain to Africa and the Balkans. Constantius held the East, and spent the 340s fighting Shapur II of Persia, who besieged the fortress city of Nisibis again and again. At Singara, in 344 or 348, the two armies fought a bloody battle that went on into the night and that neither side clearly won.

Constans was a capable soldier. In the winter of 343 he crossed the Channel to Britain, and nobody quite knows why. The brothers fell out over religion. Constans backed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and the creed of Nicaea. Constantius favoured the bishops his enemies called Arians. Constans pushed hard, even hinting at war, and in 346 Constantius let Athanasius go home.

Constans grew unpopular with his army, who found him greedy and arrogant. On 18 January 350, at a birthday banquet in Autun, a general named Magnentius walked out in the imperial purple. Constans was away hunting. He fled for Spain with a handful of followers, but horsemen caught him at Helena, near the Pyrenees, and killed him.

claims.text: Constans sailed to Britain in the depths of winter in 343.
claims.note: Firmicus Maternus and Libanius both mention the winter Channel crossing; nobody knows quite why he went.

claims.text: Magnentius was hailed at a birthday party thrown by the treasury chief Marcellinus.
claims.note: Zosimus gives the details. Other sources agree Magnentius was proclaimed at Autun in January 350.

claims.text: Constans lost the army's loyalty partly through scandal over the young men at his court.
claims.note: Aurelius Victor and Zosimus hint at it. Both are hostile, and the same charge was thrown at many unpopular rulers.

reigns.hook: Constans is dead and a usurper holds the West. One son of Constantine is left, and he's on the Persian frontier. Constantius II turns his army round and heads west.

reigns.title: Constantius II, alone
reigns.tagline: The last son standing, stiff as a statue
reigns.cameToPower: Last of the brothers left alive
reigns.previously: Magnentius seizes the West; Constans is hunted down and killed.
paragraphs: Constantius faced two rivals at once. An old general, Vetranio, had been hailed in the Balkans. Constantius met him at Naissus in December 350, talked his troops round in front of him, and let the old man retire on a pension. Magnentius was harder. At Mursa in 351 the two Roman armies tore each other apart. Magnentius lost, kept retreating, and killed himself at Lyon in 353.

Constantius was serious, suspicious and religious, backing a Christian creed that his bishops' enemies called Arian. He fought a long feud with Athanasius of Alexandria. He made his cousin Gallus a Caesar, then had him executed. In 357 he saw Rome for the first time and gawped at the Forum of Trajan like any tourist.

He needed help in Gaul, so in 355 he made Gallus's half-brother Julian a Caesar. The bookish young man turned out to be a fine general. In 360 Julian's soldiers at Paris hailed him Augustus. Constantius marched to settle it, but caught a fever on the way and died at Mopsucrene in November 361.

claims.text: Riding into Rome, Constantius stood so still that he never turned his head, spat or wiped his nose.
claims.note: Ammianus Marcellinus describes the entry of 357 in detail. He was writing within a generation and plainly enjoyed the portrait.

claims.text: On his deathbed Constantius named Julian as his heir.
claims.note: Ammianus reports it as something people said. It suited Julian very well, and nobody can check it.

claims.text: Mursa killed so many soldiers that the Roman army never recovered.
claims.note: Later writers give huge casualty figures, such as Zonaras's 54,000. Modern historians think the numbers are inflated.

reigns.hook: Constantius is dead, and the throne passes without a fight to the cousin whose family was butchered in 337. Julian rides into Constantinople, and he's finished pretending to be a Christian.

reigns.tagline: The bearded philosopher who tried to bring back the gods
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by his troops at Paris
reigns.previously: Constantius II dies of fever while marching to fight Julian.
paragraphs: Julian was about six when soldiers murdered his father in 337. He grew up under guard, buried in books, and studied in Athens. Somewhere along the way he quietly gave up Christianity for the old gods. Sent to Gaul as a Caesar, the shy scholar beat the Alamanni at Strasbourg in 357 and became the army's darling.

As emperor he reopened temples, brought back sacrifices and banned Christians from teaching the classics. He sacked swarms of palace staff and started rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem, though the work stopped. In Antioch the locals laughed at his scruffy philosopher's beard, so he wrote a satire against himself called the Misopogon, the Beard-Hater.

In 363 he invaded Persia with a huge army and reached the walls of Ctesiphon. He couldn't take it, burned his own boats and turned for home through hostile country. On 26 June, rushing into a skirmish without his armour, he took a spear in the side. He died that night, aged about 32. He left no son and named no heir.

claims.text: Julian's last words were 'You have won, Galilean.'
claims.note: It comes from the Christian historian Theodoret, writing decades later. Ammianus, who was on the campaign, gives him a calm philosopher's farewell instead.

claims.text: The spear was thrown by one of his own Christian soldiers.
claims.note: His friend Libanius said so. Ammianus, who was there, says nobody knew who threw it.

claims.text: Balls of fire burst from the ground and stopped work on the Jerusalem Temple.
claims.note: Ammianus reports the flames. An earthquake hit the region in 363, and that may lie behind the story.

reigns.hook: The army is stranded deep in Persia with no emperor, no boats and little food. The generals must choose someone tonight. They settle on a tall, cheerful guards officer called Jovian.

reigns.tagline: Eight months, one humiliating treaty, one fatal night
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by the army in Persia
reigns.previously: Julian dies of a spear wound deep in Persian territory.
paragraphs: The generals first offered the throne to the senior official Salutius, who said he was too old. Then somebody shouted for Jovian, a commander of the household guards. He was huge, friendly, fond of a drink and a Christian. His first job was getting a starving army out of Persia alive.

Shapur II made him pay for it. Jovian signed a thirty-year peace that handed Persia five provinces beyond the Tigris and the great fortress city of Nisibis, which had held out against Persian sieges for decades. Its people had to pack up and leave. Ammianus, marching home with the army, never forgave him. Jovian quietly undid Julian's pagan revival and headed for Constantinople.
He never got there. On 17 February 364, at a staging post called Dadastana in Asia Minor, he was found dead in his bed. He'd been emperor for less than eight months.

claims.text: Jovian was killed by fumes from a charcoal brazier in a freshly plastered room.
claims.note: Ammianus offers this and other explanations, including overeating, and notes that no inquiry was ever held.

claims.text: Jovian was so tall that no imperial robe could be found to fit him.
claims.note: Ammianus says so. He served in the same army, but it's the kind of detail nobody can check.

claims.text: Nisibis was handed to Persia and its citizens forced to leave.
claims.note: Ammianus describes the grief of the evacuation, and the city stayed Persian for centuries.

reigns.hook: The throne is empty again and the army is stuck in central Asia Minor. The officers argue for ten days, then choose a short-tempered Pannonian soldier named Valentinian.

reigns.title: Valentinian I & Valens
reigns.tagline: Two brothers split the world, West and East
reigns.previously: Jovian is found dead in his bed after eight months on the throne.
paragraphs: Valentinian was hailed at Nicaea in February 364. The troops demanded a colleague, so a month later he made his younger brother Valens co-emperor. They split the army and the empire between them. Valentinian took the West and spent his reign on the Rhine and the Danube, fighting the Alamanni and building forts. Valens took the East.

Valens had the rougher start. In 365 Procopius, a relative of Julian, seized Constantinople while Valens was away. Valens nearly lost his nerve, but Procopius's support melted and he was beheaded in 366. Valens then spent three years fighting the Goths across the Danube. In the West, Valentinian made his eight-year-old son Gratian co-emperor in 367.

Valentinian had a famous temper. In November 375 envoys from the Quadi came to his camp at Brigetio to apologise for a raid. As they made excuses he flew into a rage, shouting at them until he collapsed. He died within hours, probably of a stroke. His generals quickly hailed his four-year-old son Valentinian II as well.

claims.text: Valentinian kept two man-eating bears, Gold Flake and Innocence, in cages near his bedroom.
claims.note: Only Ammianus tells it, and he loathed Valentinian's cruelty. He was a contemporary, though, and gives the bears' names.

claims.text: Valentinian died of a fit of rage while shouting at envoys.
claims.note: Ammianus describes the scene in detail. Modern readers see a stroke brought on by the outburst.

reigns.hook: Valentinian is dead and his teenage son Gratian runs the West. In the East, Valens is about to face something new: a whole people of Goths on the Danube, begging to be let in.

reigns.title: Gratian & Valens
reigns.tagline: The day the Goths destroyed a Roman army
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son and brother of Valentinian I
reigns.previously: Valentinian I dies of a fit of rage at Brigetio in 375.
paragraphs: Gratian was 16 and ruled the West, with his small half-brother Valentinian II as a junior partner. His uncle Valens ruled the East. In 376 huge numbers of Goths, fleeing the Huns, arrived on the Danube and asked to come in. Valens said yes. He wanted recruits, and he got a crisis.

Roman officers in charge of the refugees robbed and starved them. Within months the Goths, led by Fritigern, were in open revolt and plundering Thrace. Gratian crushed an Alamannic army in 378 and marched east to help. Valens, by now jealous of his nephew's victories, decided not to wait.

On 9 August 378, near Adrianople, Valens attacked the Gothic wagon camp in the afternoon heat. Gothic cavalry came back from foraging and hit his flank. The Roman army was surrounded and cut to pieces. Valens died with his men, and his body was never found.

claims.text: Valens was carried wounded into a farmhouse, and the Goths burned it with him inside.
claims.note: Ammianus gives this as one of two versions. The other has him falling among the ordinary soldiers. Nobody found the body.

claims.text: Roman officers sold starving Goths dog meat in exchange for their children as slaves.
claims.note: Ammianus reports it. Roman abuse of the refugees is well attested, but the details can't be checked.

claims.text: Ammianus called Adrianople Rome's worst defeat since Cannae.
claims.note: He says so in Book 31. He also says only a third of the army escaped; the army's total size is unknown.

reigns.hook: The East has no emperor and the Goths roam the Balkans. Gratian, just 19, needs a soldier he can trust. He sends for a Spanish general living quietly in exile: Theodosius.

reigns.tagline: The last man to rule the whole Roman Empire
reigns.cameToPower: Made co-emperor by Gratian at Sirmium
reigns.previously: Valens dies at Adrianople and the Goths run loose in the Balkans.
paragraphs: Theodosius's father, a top general, had been executed in 376. The son retired to his estates in Spain until Gratian needed him. Made emperor of the East in January 379, he couldn't beat the Goths outright. In 382 he settled them inside the empire as allies under their own leaders, a deal that would shape the next century.

He was a fierce Christian. In 380 he ordered everyone to follow the Nicene creed, and in the 390s he banned pagan sacrifice. In 390 a riot in Thessalonica killed one of his generals, and Theodosius let his troops massacre thousands in the circus. Bishop Ambrose of Milan refused him communion until he did public penance, and the emperor gave in.

Gratian was murdered in 383 by the usurper Magnus Maximus, whom Theodosius beat in 388. When Valentinian II was found hanged in 392, the general Arbogast set up a puppet, Eugenius. Theodosius crushed them at the river Frigidus in 394 and briefly ruled the whole empire. He died in Milan four months later, leaving East and West to his two sons.

claims.text: At the Frigidus a miraculous wind blew the enemy's arrows back into their faces.
claims.note: Christian writers such as Rufinus and Orosius made it a miracle. That valley does get violent winds, so a real gale may lie behind it.

claims.text: Ambrose stopped Theodosius at the church door and refused to let him in.
claims.note: The dramatic doorway scene is from Theodoret, decades later. Ambrose's own letter shows he made his demand privately, in writing.

claims.text: Thousands were killed in the Thessalonica massacre.
claims.note: The massacre is well attested. Theodoret's figure of 7,000 comes later and can't be checked.

reigns.hook: The empire is split between two boys. Arcadius, 17, gets the East; Honorius, 10, gets the West. The real power in the West belongs to a half-Vandal general called Stilicho.

reigns.tagline: He hid in Ravenna while Rome was sacked
reigns.cameToPower: Inherited the West from his father
reigns.previously: Theodosius dies in Milan; the empire splits between his sons.
paragraphs: Honorius was ten, so Stilicho ran the West. The general married the emperor to his daughter Maria and, after her death, to her sister. He fought off Alaric's Goths in Italy in 402 and 403, and the court moved to Ravenna, safe behind its marshes. Then, around the end of 406, Vandals, Alans and Sueves poured across the Rhine, and a soldier in Britain declared himself Constantine III.

In 408 Honorius was persuaded Stilicho was a traitor and had him beheaded. Roman troops then slaughtered the families of barbarian soldiers, and thousands of those men went over to Alaric. Alaric marched on Rome, haggled with Honorius for two years and got nowhere. On 24 August 410 his Goths entered the city and looted it for three days, the first sack in 800 years.

Honorius never left Ravenna. His general Constantius slowly patched things up, married the emperor's sister Galla Placidia, and was briefly co-emperor before he died in 421. Honorius then fell out with Placidia, and she fled east with her children. He died in Ravenna in August 423, aged 38, with no children.

claims.text: Told that Rome had perished, Honorius panicked, thinking it meant his pet chicken named Roma.
claims.note: Procopius tells it more than a century later and admits it was just a story people repeated.

claims.text: In 410 Honorius told the cities of Britain to look to their own defence.
claims.note: Zosimus mentions the letter. Some historians think he meant Bruttium in southern Italy and got the name muddled.

reigns.hook: Honorius dies with no heir. In Rome, a senior official named Joannes is proclaimed emperor. In Constantinople, Galla Placidia and her four-year-old son are watching.

reigns.title: Joannes
reigns.tagline: The paper-pusher who grabbed the purple
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed in Rome by the army
reigns.previously: Honorius dies in Ravenna, leaving no children.
paragraphs: Joannes was the chief of the imperial notaries, a top civil servant, and he had the backing of the general Castinus. The eastern emperor Theodosius II refused to recognise him. He had his own candidate: his little cousin Valentinian, son of Galla Placidia. Joannes sent a young officer named Aetius to the Huns to hire an army.

The East moved first. A fleet and army under Ardabur and his son Aspar sailed for Italy. Ardabur was captured and held in Ravenna, where he used his time to win over Joannes's officers. Aspar's troops found a way through the marshes, and Ravenna fell. Joannes was taken to Aquileia, had a hand cut off, was paraded on a donkey in the circus, and was beheaded.
Three days later Aetius turned up with a vast Hunnic army. Placidia's side paid the Huns to go home and gave Aetius a command in Gaul.

claims.text: An angel disguised as a shepherd led the Eastern army through the marshes to Ravenna.
claims.note: Socrates Scholasticus credits Theodosius II's prayers. A local guide is the likelier explanation.

claims.text: Aetius arrived with 60,000 Huns.
claims.note: The figure comes from Philostorgius. Numbers like this in ancient writers are usually inflated.

reigns.hook: Joannes is dead and a six-year-old boy is emperor of the West. His mother will rule for him. And the general who brought the Huns is now on the payroll.

reigns.tagline: He killed his best general and paid for it
reigns.cameToPower: Installed by an army from the East
reigns.previously: Joannes is beheaded at Aquileia; the East puts a boy on the throne.
paragraphs: Valentinian was crowned in Rome at six, and his mother Galla Placidia ruled for him. Her generals fought each other. Aetius beat his rival Boniface in 432 and, with Hunnic friends behind him, became the real master of the West. Meanwhile the Vandals under Gaiseric crossed to Africa in 429 and took Carthage in 439. The West had lost its richest province.

Then came Attila. In 450 Valentinian's sister Honoria, in disgrace for an affair, sent the Hun king her ring and asked for help. Attila claimed her as his bride, with half the West as dowry. He invaded Gaul in 451 and was stopped by Aetius and the Visigoths on the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he raided Italy, met Pope Leo I, and turned back. He died in 453.

With Attila gone, Valentinian decided he no longer needed Aetius. In September 454 he stabbed the general himself during a meeting in the palace. Six months later, on 16 March 455, two of Aetius's old guardsmen cut Valentinian down while he was at archery practice on the Campus Martius in Rome.

claims.text: Pope Leo I persuaded Attila to turn away from Rome.
claims.note: Leo did meet him in 452. Disease and hunger in the Hun army were probably more persuasive. Later legend adds Saints Peter and Paul with swords.

claims.text: Honoria sent Attila her ring and asked him to rescue her.
claims.note: Priscus, a contemporary, reports it and most historians accept it, though some think the tale grew in the telling.

claims.text: A courtier told Valentinian he had cut off his right hand with his left.
claims.note: Procopius tells it a century later. A great line, but there's no earlier source.

reigns.hook: Valentinian is dead, and with him the Theodosian line in the West. A rich senator, Petronius Maximus, seizes the throne and the widowed empress. Across the sea, the Vandals are watching.

reigns.tagline: 75 days as emperor, then the Vandals arrived
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by a mob as he fled
reigns.previously: Valentinian III kills Aetius, then Aetius's men kill him.
paragraphs: Petronius Maximus had done everything a Roman aristocrat could do: twice consul, prefect of the city, prefect of Italy, and very rich. When Valentinian III was cut down on the Campus Martius in March 455, he moved fast. Within a day he was emperor. The men who had done the stabbing went unpunished.

He then forced Valentinian's widow, Licinia Eudoxia, to marry him, and married his son Palladius to her daughter Eudocia. Big mistake. Eudocia had been promised to Huneric, son of the Vandal king Gaiseric, and Gaiseric took it personally. In late May his fleet sailed for Italy. Maximus panicked and tried to run. A crowd caught him on 31 May, killed him and threw his body in the Tiber.

Days later the Vandals walked into Rome. For two weeks they stripped it at leisure: treasure, statues, half the gilded roof of the great temple on the Capitol, and thousands of captives, among them Eudoxia and her daughters. The word 'vandalism' comes from this sack, though it was only coined in the 1790s.

claims.text: Maximus plotted the murders of both Aetius and Valentinian.
claims.note: The story comes from John of Antioch, writing long after. It fits Maximus's ambition, but it reads like a palace tale and nothing else backs it up.

claims.text: Eudoxia invited Gaiseric to attack Rome to get revenge on Maximus.
claims.note: Procopius and later Byzantine writers tell it. Gaiseric had his own reasons to come, so he hardly needed an invitation.

claims.text: Pope Leo I talked Gaiseric out of burning the city and massacring its people.
claims.note: Prosper of Aquitaine, a writer from Leo's own circle, reports the meeting. The Vandals still looted for two weeks, so how much Leo saved is hard to say.

reigns.hook: Before he died, Maximus sent a Gallic noble named Avitus to the Visigoth court at Toulouse. With Rome in ruins, the Goths have an idea: why not make Avitus emperor?

reigns.tagline: The Gaul the Goths made emperor
reigns.cameToPower: Acclaimed in Gaul, with Gothic backing
reigns.reignEnded: Beaten at Piacenza, made a bishop
reigns.previously: Maximus is lynched and the Vandals sack Rome for two weeks.
paragraphs: Avitus was a grand old landowner from the Auvergne in central Gaul, a former general and prefect with long ties to the Visigoths. Their king, Theodoric II, liked the idea of a Roman emperor who owed him a favour. In July 455 Avitus was proclaimed in Gaul and headed for Italy with Gothic troops. On New Year's Day 456 his son-in-law, the poet Sidonius Apollinaris, praised him in a long verse speech in Rome.

Italy never warmed to him. Rome was hungry after the sack, and people resented paying for a Gaulish emperor and his Gothic guard. He sent the Goths home. Then two of his own officers turned on him: Majorian, and Ricimer, fresh from beating a Vandal fleet off Corsica. In October 456 they crushed his army near Piacenza. Avitus was spared and made bishop of the town, but he was dead within months.

claims.text: Short of cash, Avitus stripped bronze from Rome's public buildings and sold it.
claims.note: It comes from a fragment of John of Antioch, a hostile and much later source.

claims.text: Avitus had taught the young Theodoric II to love Roman poetry.
claims.note: Sidonius says so in his panegyric. He was Avitus's son-in-law and was paid to flatter.

claims.text: Avitus was murdered after his fall.
claims.note: Hydatius says he was killed. Gregory of Tours says he died fleeing to Gaul and was buried at Brioude, near the shrine of St Julian.

reigns.hook: With Avitus gone, the West has no emperor for over a year. Ricimer, half Sueve and half Goth, can't take the throne himself. So he backs his old comrade Majorian.

reigns.tagline: The last emperor who really tried to save the West
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed by the army, backed by Ricimer
reigns.previously: Ricimer and Majorian beat Avitus; the throne sits empty.
paragraphs: Majorian came from a military family and had served under Aetius. The army hailed him in April 457, and he was formally made emperor that December. Ricimer expected a front man. He got a worker. Majorian drove off raiders in Italy, marched into Gaul, won back Lyon and forced the Visigoths back into alliance. He passed laws against tax abuse and banned Romans from quarrying their own ancient monuments for stone.

His big plan was to finish off the Vandals. In 460 he gathered a fleet on the Spanish coast near Cartagena to invade Africa. Gaiseric struck first: helped by traitors, his ships caught the fleet at anchor and wrecked it. Majorian made peace and headed back to Italy. Ricimer had seen enough. On 2 August 461 he had the emperor seized near Tortona and stripped of his purple. Five days later Majorian was beheaded.

claims.text: Majorian slipped into Carthage in disguise, his blond hair dyed, to spy on Gaiseric.
claims.note: Procopius tells it about a century later. It has the ring of a folk tale, and no writer of the time mentions it.

claims.text: Traitors helped the Vandals destroy his invasion fleet.
claims.note: Hydatius, writing in Spain at the time, says so. Who the traitors were is unknown.

claims.text: He made it a crime to strip Rome's old public buildings for materials.
claims.note: The law survives in his collected decrees (the Novels), along with heavy fines for officials who allowed it.

reigns.hook: Ricimer has learned a lesson: never pick an emperor with ideas. His next choice is a quiet senator from southern Italy.

reigns.tagline: The emperor nobody noticed, which suited Ricimer
reigns.previously: Ricimer has Majorian arrested and beheaded at Tortona.
paragraphs: Libius Severus was a senator from Lucania in southern Italy, and that is almost all we know about him. Ricimer had him proclaimed at Ravenna in November 461 and ran the government himself. The Eastern emperor Leo I never recognised him.

The West was coming apart around them. In northern Gaul, Majorian's general Aegidius refused to accept the new regime and ruled his own patch. In Dalmatia another of Majorian's commanders, Marcellinus, did much the same. The Vandals raided Italy and Sicily year after year. Gaiseric also pushed his own candidate for the throne: the senator Olybrius, husband of Valentinian III's daughter Placidia. Severus died in Rome in November 465.

claims.text: Ricimer had him poisoned.
claims.note: Cassiodorus repeats it as hearsay. A harmless puppet was arguably more use to Ricimer alive than dead.

claims.text: Aegidius, Rome's commander in Gaul, refused to recognise him.
claims.note: Priscus and Hydatius both describe Aegidius acting on his own, even talking to the Vandals.

reigns.hook: For almost a year and a half the West has no emperor at all, and Ricimer doesn't seem to mind. But he needs Eastern ships against the Vandals, and Constantinople has a candidate.

reigns.tagline: Sent from the East, killed by his son-in-law's men
reigns.cameToPower: Sent by Leo I with an army
reigns.reignEnded: Beheaded after the siege of Rome
reigns.previously: Libius Severus dies, and the West goes without an emperor.
paragraphs: Anthemius was a Constantinople grandee: grandson of a powerful prefect, son-in-law of the late Eastern emperor Marcian, and a seasoned general. Leo I sent him west with troops, and he was proclaimed outside Rome in April 467. To seal the deal, Ricimer married his daughter Alypia. East and West were working together again, and they had one target.

In 468 a huge joint fleet sailed for Carthage under Basiliscus, brother of Leo's wife. Gaiseric asked for a five-day truce, waited for the right wind, then sent fireships into the crowded fleet off Cape Bon. The expedition was wrecked and both treasuries drained. Anthemius then lost his son Anthemiolus fighting the Visigoths in Gaul, and his quarrel with Ricimer turned poisonous.

In 472 the two went to war. Ricimer set up a rival emperor and besieged Rome for months, while hunger and disease spread in the city. In July his troops broke in. Anthemius was found and beheaded by Ricimer's nephew Gundobad.

claims.text: Gaiseric beat the great fleet by asking for a truce, then attacking with fireships.
claims.note: Procopius, writing about 80 years later, gives the fullest account. The outline isn't doubted; his numbers are.

claims.text: Anthemius hid among beggars in a church before he was caught.
claims.note: Later chroniclers tell it, but they disagree about which church, and it may be a dramatic flourish.

claims.text: Pagans hoped Anthemius would bring back the old gods.
claims.note: The pagan philosopher Damascius hints at it. Anthemius himself was openly Christian.

reigns.hook: Ricimer needed someone to crown in Anthemius's place. Constantinople had just sent one by accident: the senator Olybrius, who came as a peacemaker and stayed as a rival.

reigns.tagline: The Vandal king's pick, emperor for seven months
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed by Ricimer during a siege
reigns.previously: Ricimer turns on Anthemius and besieges him in Rome.
paragraphs: Olybrius came from the Anicii, one of Rome's richest old families, and he was married to Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III. That made him imperial family of a sort. It also made him family to the Vandals: Placidia's sister Eudocia was the wife of Gaiseric's son Huneric. Gaiseric had been pushing Olybrius for the throne for years.

In 472 Leo I sent him to Italy to patch things up between Ricimer and Anthemius. Ricimer had him proclaimed emperor instead, in April, with the siege of Rome still going on. Anthemius was dead by July. Then Ricimer died in August, and Olybrius followed him in November. Leo never recognised him.

claims.text: Leo sent Anthemius a secret letter asking him to kill Olybrius, and Ricimer intercepted it.
claims.note: Only John Malalas, a sixth-century chronicler, tells it. It's a dramatic story with nothing else to back it.

claims.text: Ricimer died vomiting blood.
claims.note: Chroniclers report it. What actually killed him is unknown.

reigns.hook: Ricimer and his emperor are both dead within three months. Ricimer's nephew Gundobad inherits the army and the kingmaking job. He picks a palace officer called Glycerius.

reigns.tagline: Deposed, then promoted to bishop
reigns.previously: Olybrius dies of dropsy, months after Ricimer.
paragraphs: Glycerius was commander of the palace guard when Gundobad had him proclaimed at Ravenna in March 473. Constantinople refused to recognise him. He did manage one success: a band of Ostrogoths threatening Italy was bought off with gifts and steered towards Gaul instead. Then Gundobad left for Burgundy to claim his share of his late father's kingdom, and Glycerius lost his protector.

Constantinople had its own man ready: Julius Nepos, the general who ruled Dalmatia. In June 474 Nepos landed at Portus, Rome's harbour, and took Glycerius without a fight. Instead of killing him, Nepos had him made bishop of Salona, on the Dalmatian coast. Glycerius went quietly.

claims.text: Glycerius was deposed and made a bishop.
claims.note: Several chronicles agree. Turning a fallen ruler into a churchman was a tidy way to end his career.

claims.text: He bribed the Ostrogoths to leave Italy for Gaul.
claims.note: Jordanes describes it, writing in the sixth century.

claims.text: Glycerius later had a hand in Nepos's murder.
claims.note: Later Byzantine sources hint at it. Nothing proves it.

reigns.hook: Julius Nepos now holds Italy, with Constantinople's blessing. To command his army he picks a man who once served as Attila's secretary. That turns out to be a mistake.

reigns.tagline: Fled Italy but never stopped being emperor
reigns.previously: Glycerius is quietly bundled off to be a bishop.
paragraphs: Nepos inherited a power base in Dalmatia from his uncle Marcellinus, the general who had refused to take orders from Ravenna. He married into the family of the Eastern empress Verina, and Constantinople sent him to Italy as its man. He took over in June 474. The West he ruled was by now little more than Italy and scraps of Gaul.

In 475 his envoys made peace with the Visigoth king Euric by handing over the Auvergne, the last Roman holdout in central Gaul. Its bishop, Sidonius Apollinaris, who had held out at Clermont through repeated sieges, was bitter. Then Nepos ordered his general Orestes to take the army to Gaul. Orestes marched on Ravenna instead. On 28 August 475 Nepos fled by sea to Dalmatia.
He never gave up the title. Constantinople went on treating him as the lawful Western emperor, and coins were still struck in his name. In 480 he was murdered by his own men in his villa near Salona.

claims.text: Sidonius felt the Auvergne had been sold out.
claims.note: His own letters say so, in some of the angriest lines he wrote.

claims.text: The ex-emperor Glycerius helped plot his murder.
claims.note: Later Byzantine sources hint at it. Nothing proves it.

reigns.hook: Orestes now holds Italy and the army. He doesn't take the crown himself. He puts it on the head of his young son.

reigns.tagline: The boy with two great names and no power
reigns.previously: Orestes turns the army on Nepos, who flees to Dalmatia.
paragraphs: His name was Romulus Augustus: Rome's founder and its first emperor rolled into one boy. People shrank it to Augustulus, 'little Augustus'. His father Orestes, once Attila's secretary, ran everything. Constantinople ignored them both and kept recognising Nepos.

Orestes was brought down by his own soldiers. The barbarian troops who made up most of Italy's army wanted land: a third of Italy's estates to settle on. Orestes refused. An officer named Odoacer promised to deliver it, and the army made him king in August 476. Orestes was caught and executed at Piacenza, and his brother Paul was killed near Ravenna. On 4 September Odoacer took Ravenna and deposed the boy.

Odoacer let Romulus live, with a pension, on an estate in Campania. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, and the Senate's envoys told the emperor Zeno that one emperor was enough for both halves. Italy had a king now. In the West, there would be no more emperors.

claims.text: Odoacer spared him because he was young and good-looking.
claims.note: The Anonymus Valesianus says so, and records a pension of 6,000 solidi. The motive is the writer's view.

claims.text: 476 was the year Rome fell.
claims.note: Marcellinus Comes, writing in Constantinople around 518, made it the end of the Western empire. At the time few noticed, and Nepos still claimed the title until 480.

claims.text: Romulus was still alive more than 30 years later.
claims.note: Cassiodorus preserves a letter from Theodoric (507–511) about a pension for a Romulus. It may or may not be him.
